Awal hari ini, JPPM membatalkan pendaftaran PN selepas mendapati penjelasan dikemukakan gabungan itu gagal menyangkal asas pembatalan yang dinyatakan dalam notis terdahulu.
Keputusan itu dibuat mengikut subperenggan 13(1)(c)(iv) Akta Pertubuhan selepas JPPM meneliti keseluruhan dokumen dan representasi dikemukakan PN pada 12 Okt.

Siasatan JPPM terhadap PN dibuat susulan aduan dilaporkan Bersatu yang mendakwa mereka dinafikan hak untuk menghadiri, memberi pendapat dan mengundi di dalam mesyuarat Majlis Tertinggi PN pada 16 Jul.

Setiausaha Agung PN Takiyuddin Hassan dilaporkan berkata gabungan itu akan mencabar pembatalan pendaftarannya dan memohon supaya pelaksanaan serta kesannya ditangguhkan sementara menunggu keputusan mahkamah.

Media melaporkan Presiden Bersatu, Muhyiddin Yassin, melahirkan rasa dukacita atas pembatalan pendaftaran PN, yang disifatkan beliau sebagai peringatan kepada pemimpin parti agar mematuhi perlembagaan dan bertindak adil.
2fe214d6629907fc: JOHOR BARU: Thirty-six foreign workers were detained at a factory in Pasir Gudang over suspicions they had used fake Malaysian identity cards to work in the country.
The group comprised eight men and 28 women aged between 16 and 45, believed to be from the Philippines and Indonesia.
They were detained during an operation by National Registration Department (NRD) personnel.
Preliminary investigations found that some of the workers had allegedly obtained the identity cards for RM100.
Some reportedly admitted to using fake identity documents bearing other people's details to secure employment.
The NRD will work with the Labour Department to investigate the factory's role and determine whether further action should be taken against the premises, Buletin Utama TV3 reported.
Investigators will also establish how the workers obtained the identity cards, it said.
a764bc2dcc57efa5: COCONUT farmer Sombat Chuekrod travelled more than 200km to join hundreds on the streets of Bangkok last Friday demanding that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank change how they deal with the developing world.

Finance ministers, central bank governors and other top policymakers had gathered in the Thai capital for the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, to tackle an inflation crisis fuelled by the United States war on Iran and other economic shocks.
The message from the IMF has been clear: after years of economic crises, worldwide debt is too high and governments need to cut spending.
For the hundreds at the protest in Bangkok, as well as for rights groups and analysts, that message is the wrong one.
"We want the IMF and World Bank to rethink their role," said 51-year-old Sombat, as he walked alongside banners demanding reform of the institutions.
"Thai people are already poor. Please don't make them any poorer."
Protest organisers called on institutions like the IMF to focus on climate financing and tax reforms that aid poorer citizens rather than demand governments cut subsidies and social spending.

"Governments across the Global South are being forced to squeeze vital spending on public health, education, and social protection just to service illegitimate debts to wealthy nations and private creditors," said Lidy Nacpil, one of the protest organisers, in a statement.

Oxfam executive director Amitabh Behar said the world was facing an "inequality emergency", and that the IMF's calls for fiscal consolidation were code for cutting spending on essential social support during the war-fuelled inflation crisis.
"It will lead to (more) price rises. It might lead to hunger."

The IMF last week upgraded its world economic outlook, citing unexpected "resilience" in economic growth. But it warned that prosperity was fragmented, with vulnerable countries falling even further behind.
It highlighted oil-importing low-income countries not exposed to the boom in artificial intelligence investment as being the most vulnerable.
Yet the IMF's advice to all countries at a time of rising global debt levels has been to cut spending and rebuild fiscal buffers after years of spending on crises.

Asked what vulnerable countries should do, IMF deputy chief of research Petya Koeva Brooks said they had "no other choice" but to address their fiscal balances by either cutting spending or increasing revenues.

The IMF has proposed making energy and food subsidies offered in the wake of the Iran war more targeted, even as the United Nations Development Programme warned that if such subsidies were cut entirely, it could plunge 130 million people into poverty.
Protest organiser Nacpil questioned in an interview how one could draw a line between who deserves a subsidy and who does not.
"How poor do you have to be for them to think that you will need some support?" she asked.
Reza Baqir of Alvarez & Marsal's Sovereign Advisory Services said he has experience with the difficult trade-offs policymakers in low-income countries face in such crises.

"During my time as Pakistan's central bank governor, I saw firsthand how difficult it can be for countries to balance the needs of the countries' citizens with the needs of the IMF programme," he said.

"At the same time, it also reinforced the importance of addressing domestic governance challenges, so countries can build their own resources and fiscal buffers, reduce their reliance on the IMF and support their citizens in a targeted and prudent manner."

Christina Segal-Knowles of the Rockefeller Foundation said developing countries are "effectively being given two bad options" — either take on debt at currently sky-high interest rates, or make extraordinary spending cuts and potentially give up on development goals.
She proposed a "growth and investment reset" that ramps up funding to countries in need as part of a set of measures designed to provide sustained support at concessional rates.
On the streets of Bangkok on Friday, protesters prepared to spend the night under a flyover.
"We are raising our voices because we believe that the network of citizens present here are key stakeholders in the negotiations," said activist Supaporn Malailoy.
"This is not merely a matter of borrowing money; it is about shaping the very structure and direction of the nation's development."

9a892035dd55c082: From Shahrim Tamrin
I welcome Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research (Miros) chairman Wong Shaw Voon’s renewed call to raise the minimum age for a motorcycle licence from 16 to 18.
But this is hardly a new proposal. It has been under discussion since 2018.
Malaysia needs neither another round of deliberations nor another announcement without a clear outcome. It needs transparency, a policy decision and the political will to act.

In May 2018, during Loke Siew Fook’s first term as transport minister, the transport ministry sought public feedback on the minimum licensing age, with Miros and relevant road safety authorities involved. The exercise ran until September, but its findings have never been made publicly available through official channels.

I obtained a summary of Miros’s findings after requesting it two years ago. The results were mixed. The online exercise involved 4,005 members of the public and 11 experts, while a separate survey covered 4,158 respondents.

Although Miros reported majority support among online participants for raising the age to 18, many motorcycle riders and secondary school students opposed the change. Some students even suggested lowering the age.
The findings do not establish a blanket public mandate for change. They establish something more fundamental: evidence was collected and the public deserves to know what became of it.

The presentation also reported that 80% of boys and 86% of girls surveyed rode to school without a motorcycle licence. Of 181 boys aged 16, only three held one. Meanwhile, 58% of students said their parents did not stop them from riding.

These figures concern the students surveyed, not all Malaysian schoolchildren. Nevertheless, they expose a problem that raising the licensing age alone cannot solve. Even a 13-year-old can ride an illegally obtained “kapcai”.
Wong himself has cautioned that raising the age will achieve little without effective enforcement against underage riders.
Licensing reform must, therefore, go hand in hand with enforcement, parental accountability and controls over access to motorcycles.
The paper trail

On Oct 8, 2019, police proposed a new B3 motorcycle licensing category at the National Road Safety Council’s 60th annual general meeting. The proposal envisaged restricting young riders to motorcycles of 70cc or below, or low-powered electric alternatives, to curb illegal street racing and improve road safety.

Recorded as Item 9.4 in the meeting minutes, the proposal was referred to the transport ministry. Years later, the public is still waiting to learn whether it was seriously considered and why it produced no clear policy outcome.

On Nov 25, 2021, Miros’s board backed a related but distinct proposal to study restricting young riders to motorcycles below 90cc. Recorded as Board Paper LPM 2-52 under Item 52.4(2), it was approved by the board, including its then chairman Suret Singh.
One proposal concerned a licensing category; the other concerned research into engine-capacity restrictions.
Nearly five years later, the study’s status remains unclear. Was it completed? What did it find? Were recommendations submitted to the transport ministry? If the study was not completed, why not?

In August 2024, the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (Suhakam) children’s commissioner Farah Nini Dusuki sought an update on the B3 proposal and urged the transport ministry and road transport department (JPJ) to expedite legislation addressing motorcycle purchases by unlicensed riders. She also highlighted the unresolved status of the Miros study.
A study endorsed by the board should not become an administrative mystery.
Human cost
Suhakam has highlighted the risks faced by underage motorcyclists, including 87 children aged six to 10 who died while riding motorcycles rather than as pillion passengers.
Children do not acquire motorcycles by themselves. Adults may purchase them, provide access or knowingly permit illegal riding. Sellers and the wider regulatory framework also warrant scrutiny.

Section 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001 addresses neglect likely to cause physical injury to a child, while Section 39(5) of the Road Transport Act 1987 addresses causing or permitting a child below 16 to drive. Their application depends on the circumstances and relevant legal requirements.
Parental accountability matters, but it must not become a substitute for institutional accountability.

The government should disclose the status of legislation reportedly being developed to regulate motorcycle purchases by unlicensed individuals, explain outstanding obstacles and provide a timetable. The problem extends beyond teenagers riding kapcai – unlicensed adults can also access more powerful motorcycles.
I call on the transport ministry, JPJ and Miros to:
Publish the 2018 survey. Release its methodology, detailed findings and recommendations, while protecting respondents’ personal information where necessary.
Account for Board Paper LPM 2-52. Confirm whether the study was completed, publish its findings and explain what action followed.
Disclose the proposed legislation’s status. Set a timetable for regulating motorcycle purchases by unlicensed buyers and establish enforceable safeguards.

Set a timetable for licensing reform. Decide whether to raise the minimum age to 18 and seriously consider the B3 proposal, alongside proportionate power restrictions for young and inexperienced riders, effective enforcement and meaningful parental accountability.
Wong deserves credit for returning the issue to the agenda. In my years covering Miros, I have seen board recommendations stall before reaching the ministerial table.
It remains unclear whether Board Paper LPM 2-52, or any recommendation arising from it, ever reached the transport minister in a form requiring a decision. That, too, warrants an explanation.

Research cannot improve road safety if recommendations fail to travel from the boardroom to the ministerial table. Nor can policy succeed if it exists only in announcements, meeting minutes and presentation slides.
Malaysia is not short of studies, recommendations or press statements. It is short of visible follow-through.
Publish the evidence. Account for the decisions made and those left unmade. Set a timetable and act. The public has waited long enough, and too many children have already paid the price.
Shahrim Tamrin is a sustainable transport and road safety activist and former Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research board member.

563d51871bb60e96: Surprisingly few organizations were promoting Linux distros at Open Source Summit Europe. The only dedicated stands we found belonged to two Chinese projects, with openEuler occupying the larger booth.

For users accustomed to Western enterprise distros, openEuler may be a less familiar name, but it has an impressive history. It's the modern free community version of Huawei's EulerOS, a version of which achieved official official UNIX™ certification. openEuler is no longer a solely Huawei project, though. Since then, it's been opened up, and it is now run by the OpenAtom Foundation.

OpenAtom was co-founded in 2020 by Huawei along with some other big Chinese names, such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent. Another of the co-founders was Inspur, which formerly developed its own distro, K/UX – a version of which also achieved official UNIX™ certification.

Inspur K/UX won Unix certification in February 2016, and EulerOS seven months later. K/UX's Unix certification expired in 2019. A few months later, in May 2019, the US placed wider sanctions on Huawei. It is possible that the fresh restrictions on American sales prompted Huawei's interest in closer co-operation with other companies in the Chinese Linux space. As far as we can see, there were no further versions of K/UX after version 3. As additional motivation for cooperation, both EulerOS and K/UX were originally based on CentOS Linux, and of course, in December 2020, the CentOS Project announced it would shift its focus from CentOS Linux to CentOS Stream.

The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM. It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler. As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant).

Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download. Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler.

openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle, akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024, while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page: the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. As LWN put it last year, this is a "non-upstream kernel port."

There are five types of installation ISO available: Offline Standard, Offline Everything (a hefty 24.9 GB), Network Install (a still significant 1.5 GB), and two variants of the desktop "DevStation" version – a basic one at 3.3 GB and an "everything" edition at 25 GB.

We gave the DevStation a very quick whirl in VirtualBox. It boots into its own installation program called Heolleo, which offers the choice of Simplified Chinese or English. Installation took a while, as it automatically fetches updates as it goes. We ended up with a GNOME desktop configured for Chinese, but we opened Settings, typed "language" into the Search box, and picked English. After a reboot, we could read most of the desktop. Program groups and some other elements are still in Chinese, but it's navigable with a bit of guesswork. It's GNOME 49, with the Dash to Panel and Arc Menu extensions preinstalled for a slightly more familiar layout. Opening a terminal, we were greeted with:
It also offers the Deepin Desktop Environment, UKUI (as seen in Ubuntu Kylin), MATE, Xfce, and the Kiran Desktop Environment, which is a new one to us.

In places, the English-language materials for openEuler mention Chinese CPU makers rather than western ones – which is understandable, in context. Examples include processors from Hygon, a Chinese licensee of AMD designs, as well as Phytium and Kunpeng, which explain the Arm support on offer.

In the western world, the Red Hat user community responded to the end of CentOS Linux by building new free distros that stay as close as they can to their progenitor: the Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux projects, rebuilt from Red Hat source code.

Then, when the IBM subsidiary restricted access to that source to its customers in 2023, the Rocky and AlmaLinux projects started to diverge. Rocky aims for the closest possible RHEL compatibility, and its most visible innovation is that it's built its own new build service. It also found a clever workaround to get Red Hat's kernel source code. AlmaLinux still targets RHEL compatibility, but differentiates itself by retaining older device support and older CPU architectures after Red Hat drops them.

Chinese vendors have responded very differently. Those offering CentOS Linux-based OSes clubbed together, dropped their rival versions and their UNIX compatibility efforts, and instead are working on new tools and subsystems. Much like European interest in digital sovereignty, this is in part due to the Trump administration. Half a decade after it was cut off from its upstream sources, the openEuler platform is thriving and growing, even if few in the western world pay any attention at all. ®
2821d70d5a348f2a: JAKARTA: Indonesians protested in several cities on Tuesday, raging against wildfires and a toxic haze that has made thousands unwell for weeks on end in a crisis that has engulfed Southeast Asia.
Demonstrations were called by students to display dissatisfaction with the government of president Prabowo Subianto, which marked its second year on Tuesday.

They railed against perceived ineptitude and corruption during protests in the capital Jakarta, but also in Bandung and Yogyakarta elsewhere on Java island, as well as Pekanbaru in Sumatra and Makassar in South Sulawesi.
Many pointed particularly to an inability to put out the fires that have ravaged vast swaths of Borneo and Sumatra islands since July.
"If we burn, you burn with us!" read a protest banner held up by a demonstrator in Jakarta.
"I have the right to breathe. Extinguish the fires immediately," said another.
Residents in the city of Palangkaraya, on Borneo, told AFP of their despair.
"This haze is really bad. Sales are quiet. Prices keep going up, but there's no income," said Melsi, a 40-year-old streetside drinks vendor.
She cried as she spoke to AFP.
"What can we do? We're the little people, we can't do anything but hope that the government will handle it," Melsi said.
'Beaten up'
Homemaker Sifra, 29, said her husband and two children have been coughing for a month.
"Even inside the house, the smoke gets in. Honestly, since the haze, my body aches, as if I've been beaten up. The immune system is down. I get coughs and colds easily," she said.

Sifra, who like many Indonesians has one name, urged the government to step up its efforts - echoing the call made by dozens who protested in Palangkaraya on Monday to demand the declaration of a state of emergency.

Police detained six activists who had draped Greenpeace protest banners from a monument on Jakarta's central Bundaran HI roundabout on Tuesday morning, before the student marches, according to Jeanny Sirait, a campaigner for the NGO.
One read: "Haze & Prabowo's Regime = National Disaster."
National Disaster Mitigation Agency spokesman Berton Panjaitan told journalists in the capital that more than 60,000 firefighters, including volunteers, were deployed in dousing efforts countrywide.
Forty-nine aircraft were available for water bombing and cloud seeding to make rain, although many have been grounded intermittently due to the haze.
The Nusantara Atlas wildfire monitor said on Monday the Indonesian blazes have burned more than 1.9 million hectares of land in the first nine months of 2026.
The fires have sent air pollution levels soaring as far afield as Kuala Lumpur and Singapore.
Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe, partly due to a particularly severe episode of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
a2992e89e4dd0443: PETALING JAYA: Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja'afar dan empat individu yang mendakwa diri mereka sebagai undang Negeri Sembilan mempertikaikan pembatalan pelantikan 10 ahli Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri (exco) pada bulan lepas.

Tunku Nadzaruddin menegaskan semula dakwaan beliau terhadap takhta, malam tadi, dengan mendakwa Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir bukan lagi Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan apabila pelantikan ahli-ahli exco berkenaan dibatalkan pada 20 Sept, maka tidak sah dan tidak berperlembagaan.

"Kami dengan ini mengurniakan limpah perkenan kepada Ismail Lasim selaku menteri besar dan barisan exco... untuk terus mengemudi pentadbiran kerajaan Negeri Sembilan," menurut kenyataan bersama dengan empat 'undang' berkenaan dan Tunku Besar Tampin.

Mereka mendakwa Tuanku Muhriz bukan lagi Yang Dipertuan Besar apabila suatu proklamasi sebelum ini, oleh individu yang mendakwa diri mereka sebagai undang, diterima dan diputuskan untuk 'dilaksanakan' oleh exco.
Negeri Sembilan tidak mempunyai barisan exco sejak 20 Sept lalu selepas 10 anggotanya dilucutkan jawatan kerana melanggar sumpah jawatan.
Pemecatan itu dibuat susulan kenyataan mereka lima hari sebelumnya yang menyokong satu pengisytiharan untuk menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar.

Mereka terdiri daripada wakil Umno, iaitu Mustapha Nagoor (Palong); Faizal Ramli (Linggi); Zaiful Bahri Idris (Chembong); Razi Ali (Sungai Lui); Asna Amin (Lenggeng); Siti Nur Umaira Hasim (Labu); dan Suhaimizan Bizar (Gemencheh).
Tiga lagi terdiri daripada wakil MCA Siow Kong Choon (Chennah); Fairuz Isa daripada PAS (Serting); serta Razali Abu Samah (Sikamat) daripada Wawasan.
Pembatalan pelantikan 10 exco berkenaan diwartakan pada 24 Sept.

Sebelum ini, Dewan Undangan dan Keadilan Negeri Sembilan menegaskan keputusan exco berhubung penurunan takhta Tuanku Muhriz tidak mempunyai kesan undang-undang kerana perkara itu di luar bidang kuasa kerajaan negeri.

Setiausaha Raja Norazli Raja Nordin berkata perkara berkaitan adat Melayu, termasuk pemilihan, pelantikan, peletakan dan pemecatan Yang Dipertuan Besar serta Undang, terletak dalam bidang kuasanya menurut Perkara XVI Undang-undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan (UUTKNS).

Mengenai proklamasi pula, Jabatan Peguam Negara menarik perhatian kepada pandangan awalnya bahawa proklamasi 19 April itu adalah tidak sah kerana tidak mematuhi kehendak-kehendak mandatori Perkara 10 UUTKNS.
a1bd1920d6256523: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia hopes Japan will continue providing defence assistance under its Official Security Assistance (OSA) programme in 2027 and beyond, with an expanded scope to strengthen the country's defence capabilities.
Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said the matter was discussed during his meeting with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi on the third day of his working visit to Japan.

He said Malaysia expressed its appreciation to the Japanese government for assistance provided under the programme, including the supply of counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (counter-UAV) systems to Malaysia.

"Both sides also exchanged views on security developments in the Indo-Pacific, particularly the situation in the South China Sea, with Malaysia emphasising the importance of Asean unity in addressing regional security challenges and preserving peace and stability in the region," he said in a Facebook post.

The meeting also covered efforts to expand maritime cooperation, explore government-to-government (G2G) defence procurement arrangements and a proposal to hold annual meetings between the defence ministers of both countries, following his meeting with his Japanese counterpart yesterday.

Khaled said the discussions also touched on the longstanding educational ties between the two countries, including the establishment of the Malaysia-Japan International Institute of Technology (MJIIT) and the University of Tsukuba campus in Malaysia, in line with the spirit of the Look East Policy.

He added that Malaysia regarded Japan as a trusted strategic partner, with bilateral ties expected to strengthen further ahead of the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries in 2027.
4584e69ce7546bd6: PETALING JAYA: Bersatu has been accused of engineering Perikatan Nasional’s (PN) deregistration after losing its leadership positions, allegedly to pave the way for an alliance with Pakatan Harapan (PH).
Wawasan leader Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal accused Bersatu of betraying its coalition partner PAS by lodging the complaint that led to PN’s deregistration today.
“People know the real cause was Bersatu’s complaint after its leaders were democratically removed from their positions in PN,” the Machang MP said in a statement.
He accused Bersatu’s leaders of shedding crocodile tears over the decision, alleging they pursued a “scorched-earth” strategy to bring down the coalition rather than surrender control to PAS.
Wan Fayhsal pointed to negotiations between Bersatu and the PH-led Selangor government over a confidence and supply agreement as evidence of an emerging political realignment.

Earlier today, Selangor menteri besar Amirudin Shari said he would review the state government’s planned cooperation with Bersatu following PN’s deregistration, but insisted the arrangement would be with Bersatu and not PN.
Wan Fayhsal claimed similar cooperation was being explored in Melaka.

He also questioned the timing of the Registrar of Societies’ (RoS) decision to cancel PN’s registration, which came two days before a court hearing on an application to stay the coalition’s suspension.
"Why such a rush that they could not even wait another two days?" he asked.
Wan Fayhsal accused RoS of double standards, claiming it ignored complaints over Bersatu’s internal disputes but acted swiftly when the party complained about PN.
He also accused the Madani government of using administrative powers to weaken political opponents ahead of the Melaka state election and GE16.
He, however, did not address Bersatu’s claim that it was excluded from PN’s Supreme Council meeting on July 16.
Bersatu secretary-general Azmin Ali had earlier accused the PAS-led PN leadership of breaching the coalition's constitution by denying Bersatu the right to attend, speak and vote at the meeting.
Azmin maintained that Bersatu’s complaint to RoS was intended to ensure PN complied with its constitution.
385eb8427c27947d: PETALING JAYA: Police have arrested two men after rescuing a 16-year-old girl believed to have been a victim of sexual exploitation in Arau, Perlis, last night.
State police chief Hamzah Hashim said a raid was conducted on a premises in Arau at 11.15pm following investigations and intelligence work.
He said in a statement the two suspects were believed to have promoted prostitution activities on a social media application and exploited the girl for sexual purposes.

The case is being probed for trafficking in children under Section 14 of the Anti-Trafficking In Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Act and exploiting a person for prostitution under Section 372 of the Penal Code.
71a68cf191db87b9: ANKARA: Turkey have appointed Sergen Yalcin as head coach on a four-year contract to replace the sacked Italian Vincenzo Montella, the country's football federation (TFF) announced on Tuesday.
The 53-year-old former Turkey midfielder steps into the job following Montella's dismissal earlier this month after a difficult Uefa Nations League campaign.
Turkey sit bottom of Group A1 after four consecutive losses, having also suffered a group stage exit from the 2026 World Cup.
"We wish Yalcin success in his new role and hope this decision proves auspicious for our country and our national team," the TFF said in a statement.
A prominent figure in Turkish football, Yalcin won 37 caps from 1994 to 2003, featured at Euro 1996 and Euro 2000 and played for Besiktas, Fenerbahce, and Galatasaray.
As a manager, Yalcin guided Besiktas to a domestic double of the Super Lig and Turkish Cup in the 2020–2021 season.
He ended a second stint in charge of Besiktas in May.
cd31a4d7c5db02f0: Seasoned techies recall with nostalgia a simpler time when the “single-stack” model of enterprise computing held as the default approach to solving interoperability headaches.

Back then IT decision-makers were prepared to forfeit some choice and flexibility in how they specified IT systems in return for the availability and manageability that came with a homogenous operating environment.

With the subsequent rise of multi-clouds, application-specific hardware, ever-changing business requirements, and the race for AI, the old “one-size-fits-all” playbook has been largely abandoned. Most IT estates have embraced technological diversity, some by design, some through standardization, some by inertia.
Modern enterprise environments have become innately heterogeneous – and innately complex. They run a diverse combo of system software, hardware devices, cloud services, legacy applications, et al.

The advance of AI has brought standard CPUs, specialized GPUs, fast networking fabrics, distributed data pipelines, and new deployment models that span private clouds, public clouds, edge – and ever-pressing ROI expectations.

But that doesn’t mean that companies’ existing applications and data simply disappear. One trying but inevitable outcome of rapid AI deployment is the so-called “VM-container divide”. This is where critical business applications tipped to transition to containers continue to run on virtual machines, because cloud-native services are taking precedence, nabbing container and Kubernetes availability. So companies face the challenge of operationalizing AI, without being forced into complex migrations or creating new infrastructure silos.

Dealing with this technological schism poses acute challenges for IT management. Many new AI deployments are going straight to containers, while existing data and applications – which the AI needs to access – continue to run on VMs.

Running separate stacks for VMs and containers creates a number of issues, such as duplicate capacity plans, separate support contracts, and fragmented governance. And after years of trying to get beyond the pitfalls of siloed data, exasperated enterprises are now having to deal with siloed infrastructure.

Separately managed VM and container environments often mean inefficient resource utilization. This in turn can lead to “stranded capacity” – installed computing resources that cannot be used to support live workloads. VM clusters are frequently underutilized while container pools (like Kubernetes) are overprovisioned, with no easy way to share resources without manual intervention.

Furthermore, VM/container infrastructure fragmentation can create an operations bottleneck for agentic AI. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. When AI agents cannot autonomously communicate across environments, their utility droops from autonomous problem-solvers to plain localised macros.

Containers are gaining because of the widespread embrace of AI-enabled applications. Eighty-five percent of IT executives polled by Nutanix’s most recent Enterprise Cloud Index survey think that AI is accelerating their organization’s adoption of containers in a meaningful way; 29 percent think it is speeding-up adoption “to a great extent”.

“AI is accelerating the shift to containers because machine learning models require strict dependency packing, while critical applications and data remain spread across both virtualised and containerised environments,” says Harsha Kotikela, Senior Director of Product & Solutions Marketing at Nutanix.

Agents are multi-tier by nature he explains. “Inference is typically GPU-intensive and container-based, while agents are often CPU-intensive and container-based, and existing enterprise applications and data largely remain in VM environments. The challenge is to bring these tiers together so agents can work with enterprise applications and data, without forcing migration or creating additional infrastructure silos.”

The application landscape, meanwhile, has become just as diverse. Many organisations simultaneously operate traditional enterprise applications running on VMs, containerised apps, distributed AI applications and intelligent agents, with workloads deployed across private cloud, public cloud, and edge. Each environment has its own management tools, operational processes, security rules and governance models.

“Management capability has struggled to scale up commensurately,” says Kotikela, but adding more consoles or building separate operational teams for every technology stack does not necessarily solve this complexity: “In many cases, it increases it.”

However, Kotikela challenges the notion that the predicament enterprises face in straddling the VM-container divide is intractable. Rather, the challenge is to move towards a unified operating model that allows them to operationalize agentic AI while retaining flexibility across their existing and new environments.

“Rather than trying to work around heterogeneity, the objective now should be to make heterogeneous environments operate consistently with purposeful policies,” Kotikela says. “This is where Nutanix's dual-native architecture comes in, enabling enterprises to operationalize agentic AI across container-based inference and agent workloads alongside existing VM-based applications and data, through a consistent operating model.”

The reality is that the VM-to-container migration trend is sluggish, Kotikela suggests. Few enterprises are starting from scratch with containers. Many have long-established business applications on legacy architectures, on top of which they are building container-based applications, but mostly not to replace what they already have running on VMs. Rather, they are prolonging their VM investment.

It’s customer interest that’s informed how Nutanix provisions a governed, dual-native architecture through its Nutanix Cloud Platform – NCP – which runs traditional VMs and containerised/Kubernetes-based AI workloads concurrently on a single, consistent infrastructure.

NCP’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure foundation unifies compute, storage, virtualisation and management across on-premises resources, public clouds and edge. It works in concert with Nutanix Enterprise AI (NAI), which provides the software capabilities to deploy, govern, and scale AI workloads.

Technology partnerships are vital to building AI support functionality into Nutanix's AI portfolio, explains Kotikela. “Nutanix and NVIDIA work together to provide an integrated platform for enterprise AI, combining Nutanix’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure and software with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI software. Nutanix Enterprise AI simplifies the deployment, management, and secure operation of AI models, integrating with NVIDIA NIM and NeMo microservices to support enterprise AI inference and agentic AI workflows.”

Meanwhile, “Nutanix Kubernetes Platform provides the foundation for managing Kubernetes environments, while Nutanix Unified Storage delivers the high-performance data access required by AI workloads. Together, these capabilities help enterprises deploy and scale AI while maintaining control over their infrastructure, models, and data.”
Stacks of opportunity

“In an ideal IT world you do not want to have to manage two different operational stacks – but the world of IT is rarely ‘ideal’,” Kotikela points out. “So you have to approach the challenge from a realistic perspective. You cannot bend your current stacks to a different reality without the risk of something breaking, and there’s no sense in that.”

He adds: “A platform that unifies VMs and containers improves developer time-to-value by getting rid of those infrastructure silos, and providing a single control plane.” Rather than development teams having to manage separate pipelines for existing VMs and containerised applications, a unified platform “treats both as services of equal status and importance”.

NAI delivers a unified and secure platform to deploy, manage and scale AI workloads, Kotikela says. It gives enterprises governance over their agents and models, full visibility over token usage, and streamlines AI development with a straightforward interface that integrates with existing infrastructure.”
Giving agents agency

According to Kotikela the next phase of agentic AI will be measured by the ability to operate agents with governance, visibility and control: “That’s what we set out to solve with the newest NAI release. Release 2.8 continues to evolve NAI with new control and governance capabilities across Nutanix Agent Gateway and Nutanix Private Inference. This means organisations can run AI across VMs and containers, bridge public-cloud LLMs with private self-hosted models, and deploy AI where data already is.”

Kotikela adds: “When I speak to customers, they tell me they want the freedom to choose between frontier and open-source models based on performance and cost, as well as the flexibility to run AI workloads in the cloud for experimentation and move them on-premises when they need greater control over their data or have sovereignty requirements.”
Stitch in time

For Kotikela the biggest challenge going forward is “operationalizing agentic AI - bringing together all the components required to make it work - from GPUs and underlying infrastructure to Kubernetes, AI models, inference engines, and gateways. These components must work together seamlessly across cloud, on-premises, and edge environments. Integrating and operating this multi-tier architecture requires significant time and effort from developers, IT architects, and infrastructure teams, diverting resources from delivering business outcomes.”

This is where Nutanix delivers value, says Kotikela. “We’ve done the heavy lifting of bringing together the infrastructure and software components required to run Agentic AI - within a unified operating model across hybrid environments. This allows IT teams to focus less on integrating and managing the underlying stack and more on operationalizing AI to deliver business value.”

d803cd30290c796e: LONDON: Prince Harry has said he hoped to reconcile with King Charles and the rest of his family with whom he fell out when he moved to the United States six years ago.

Harry, 42, the king's younger son, caused a huge rupture in the British royal family when he and his wife Meghan quit royal duties and moved to California in 2020 from where they were highly critical of the institution.
He has barely spoken to his older brother, heir Prince William, for years, and his family has only recently met up again with his father.
In an interview with GQ magazine, Harry, who recently relocated back to Britain with Meghan and their two children, said he wanted to patch things up.
"With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile," he told GQ.
He said he could understand the fascination with his family's situation as people could relate to it.
"There's sibling disagreements, there's broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent," he said.
Some people might be inspired by efforts to reconcile and this could help their own relationships.
"And some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out," he added.
Harry's spokesperson said those latter comments were not meant as a swipe at William or any other family members.
Harry, the Duke of Sussex, went on to tell GQ that while "scars stick around forever", he wanted to encourage everybody to let go of the past.
"For me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives than to continue with issues with family," he said. "It's not worth it."
In the lengthy interview, Harry also discussed themes he has previously talked about, such as the impact of losing his mother Princess Diana when he was 12 and his mental health struggles.

"I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they've been in school for two weeks. They're loving it and it's just giving them a whole different experience."

"My hope is that it will change," he said. "There have been some battles that have been fought, necessarily so. But hopefully we can all draw a line under that.

453597ae6c05a579: JAKARTA: Indonesians protested in several cities on Tuesday, raging against wildfires and a toxic haze that has made thousands unwell for weeks on end in a crisis that has engulfed Southeast Asia.
Demonstrations were called by students to display dissatisfaction with the government of President Prabowo Subianto, which marked its second year on Tuesday.

They railed against perceived ineptitude and corruption during protests in the capital Jakarta, but also in Bandung and Yogyakarta elsewhere on Java island, as well as Pekanbaru in Sumatra and Makassar in South Sulawesi.

Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe, partly due to a particularly severe episode of the El Nino weather phenomenon.

fed74bf54807e3db: PETALING JAYA: The government bars artificial intelligence (AI) service providers from using data from the government or the people to train their AI models, says digital minister Gobind Singh Deo.

In a written parliamentary reply, Gobind said this is a clause in all of the government's AI procurement contracts, adding that AI firms are also not allowed to store data from Malaysians after processing.
"The guidelines on AI use in the public sector also makes it mandatory for all government agencies to minimise, conceal or anonymise data before processing them with AI systems," he said.
He added that the ministry is drafting an AI governance bill to ensure accountability when it comes to AI systems.
The minister was responding to Ahmad Fadhli Shaari (PN-Pasir Mas) who asked how the government was ensuring public data processed by cloud and AI firms remain under Malaysia's control.
Only non-sensitive, open data stored in foreign clouds

Gobind said the government only stores non-sensitive, open data in foreign-based data clouds, while secret and top secret government data can only be stored in government data centres, not just any online cloud.
On the other hand, confidential and restricted information can only be stored in personal or hybrid clouds based in Malaysia, he said.
"For personal data handled by the private sector, relocating it to foreign clouds is regulated by Section 129 of the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), as amended in 2024," he said.

Among others, the amended section requires consent to be granted by subjects for the cross-border transfer of their personal data, while receiving jurisdictions must have a law similar to Malaysia's PDPA in place.

Gobind said the government also mandates encryption of its data to ensure foreign service providers are incapable of unilaterally accessing the data, even if requested by the authorities of other nations.
00ca37e120856345: FRANCE is counting the cost of some of its worst unrest in years at the weekend over the cost of living and under-funded public services.
HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT STOP MORE VIOLENCE AND HELP VICTIMS?
Authorities say 2,500 people are in custody awaiting questioning while 149 are detained awaiting trial.
Partial curfews have been imposed in parts of Paris, Bordeaux, Lille, Lyon, Nice and Marseille to keep the streets quiet in areas worst-hit by rioting.
The government, which had 60,000 officers mobilised at the weekend, plans to increase police numbers on the ground.
For businesses and victims of violence, the government is implementing state-financed furlough measures to avoid layoffs, and providing funds to help companies meet cashflow needs.
Insurers have promised speedy payouts to cover some of the damage, which hit more than 3,000 shops.
HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT ADDRESS UNDERLYING COMPLAINTS?
France's extremely strained public finances mean the government has precious little room for broader measures to address protesters' anger over the rising cost of living.
It has already hiked emergency spending this year to help certain sectors like farmers, fishermen and haulers cope with high fuel costs caused by the Iran war.
The ​protests began last month at high schools in Paris' ​working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and ⁠shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement.
The government has so far not committed to substantial extra funding for schools but has pledged to send some 3,000 teachers, who are qualified but not yet working, to fill staffing gaps.
HAVE PROTESTS PEAKED?

Cities were quieter at the start of the week. But some protesters have called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday. Unions have called for strikes on November 5 to protest budget cuts and support hiking wages.
Schools are on a break for two weeks, but some student organisations are calling for more demonstrations.
HOW WILL FRANCE'S DIRE ECONOMIC SITUATION BE AFFECTED?
The unrest is a blow to business confidence, which was already fragile due to a fiscal crisis and high energy prices.

The minority government is struggling to pass spending cuts in a divided parliament as part of its 2027 budget and is at risk of being toppled by opposition parties if a compromise cannot be found with at least some of them.
The government wants to cut its budget deficit to five per cent of economic output next year from 5.4 per cent this year – one of the biggest in the euro zone.
French bond yields climbed further on Tuesday after their biggest daily rise in nearly a month in the previous session, with investors remaining cautious.
The yield on France's 10-year benchmark bond reached 4.96 per cent at one point on Tuesday.
WILL THE UNREST SPREAD TO OTHER COUNTRIES?
If France cannot contain the unrest, there is a risk that it could spill across its borders with deep public anger around Europe over cost-of-living issues.
In neighbouring Italy, clashes erupted between police and protesters on Sunday.
Albania has also seen a series of student demonstrations in recent days over corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, while Spain and Portugal have faced protests over housing.
HOW WILL THE UNREST AFFECT THE 2027 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION?
Elections next year will see President Emmanuel Macron step down after a decade in power.
The unrest is likely to boost far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in polls and has long talked tough on law and order.
"Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign," Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron's camp, told Reuters.
"It's not just a clear path ahead of her, it's a six-lane highway."
Hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has come under pressure for backing protesters' demands, criticising the government's handling and not clearly condemning the violence.
Meanwhile, Macron, who headed off to the Middle East on Monday, has emerged from the crisis further weakened.
His former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, now a centre-right presidential candidate, said on X he wanted "decisions and initiatives" from the lame-duck leader to "restore order."
ARE PARIS AND OTHER CITIES SAFE TO VISIT?

There have been no reports of any injuries to foreigners caught up in the unrest. However, several European governments advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution.
* The article is from Reuters

d638d300d1e4a46a: Enterprises say nearly a third of their software budgets goes on upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes they wouldn't have chosen, according to research suggesting that keeping vendors happy has become an expensive business.

The study, conducted by Censuswide for software support provider Origina and published with Thinkers50, surveyed 2,018 senior IT decision-makers in the US and UK. Respondents put the average share at 28 percent.

And customers aren't necessarily getting anything better for their money. Some 95 percent of respondents said they had paid for at least one vendor-driven change in the past three years despite expecting worse reliability, performance, or value.
The most recent vendor-driven change cost respondents' organizations an average of $12.87 million.
Origina calls this the "software tax," but unlike most taxes, it comes with the added pleasure of potentially making your IT systems worse.

The costs don't stop at software either. According to the survey, 91 percent of respondents said their organizations had retired working hardware in the past three years to meet software support deadlines, sacrificing an estimated 1.65 years of remaining useful life on average.

Then there's the small matter of finding people to carry out all these supposedly essential changes. Some 84 percent said experienced engineers were regularly diverted from other projects to handle vendor-driven upgrades and migrations.

That leaves less time for the work businesses actually want done, including the AI projects that software vendors themselves have spent the past few years telling everyone they urgently need. Asked about the last time an AI or data project was delayed, paused, or canceled, 90 percent said vendor-driven costs contributed at least moderately.

While customers might be tempted to tell their suppliers where to stick their next upgrade, many apparently don't feel they have much choice. Some 76 percent said they have little negotiating leverage with their major software vendors.
Origina founder and CEO Tomás O'Leary reckons customers have been backed into a corner.

"When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response. That's exactly the problem," he said. "The market has left some of the most experienced technology leaders in the world with little room to refuse, and that cost shows up in budgets, in engineering time and in innovation that never gets funded."

The findings also suggest that IT bosses are getting rather fed up with the arrangement. Some 91 percent backed legislation that would give enterprise software customers protections comparable to those enjoyed by long-term residential tenants, while 82 percent supported software maintenance requirements similar to EU hardware repairability rules.
Origina has a commercial interest in the argument: it sells independent support for enterprise software, offering customers an alternative to vendors' own maintenance and upgrade arrangements.
Still, the findings suggest plenty of customers feel they're spending millions following their suppliers' priorities rather than their own. ®

2da903bad9cde08b: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon.

This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover.
Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year.
Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform.

Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole.
What we know about SBC4 so far

The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it.
No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried.

What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat.

Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up.

Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data.
However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running.

Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body.
Not only do HPE’s systems power some of the fastest supercomputers on Earth, but they could soon hold the number one spot on the Moon — not that that’s a particularly high bar.

Beyond bragging rights, a workload like HPL could have other benefits like helping to keep the rover from icing over during the roughly 14-day-long night cycles the rover will repeatedly endure over the course of its mission.
Hardening SBC4 for the Moon

The Rover and by extension SBC4 will have to contend with extreme vibration stresses during launch and landing, wild temperature swings, not to mention cosmic rays and solar radiation since the Moon lacks the thick atmosphere and magnetic field that shields terrestrial compute.
But, as it turns out, radiation might not be as big a problem as you’d think. According to Fernandez, SBC4 is largely assembled from off-the-shelf components, including the solid state drives.
The compute platform is using standard Kioxia BG6 M.2 drives with the main line of protection being a software RAID 1.

“It’s a silent mirror. The boot order is to try this and if something has happened to it, go here,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space tech and solutions, explained. “With our nine years' experience in the Space Station using drives, we’ve even convinced them we don’t need to do anything special for space.”

However, this wasn’t always the thinking. As we reported at the time, early Spaceborne Computers suffered from high SSD failure rates. But as it turned out, so did the same drives deployed terrestrially. The cause of the failures wasn’t cosmic rays or energetic particles from the Sun, but rather bad capacitors, he explained. “I’ve had zero SSD failure since 2019.”
While off-the-shelf electronics are surprisingly radiation resistant — at least within FLIP’s mission parameters — HPE has invested heavily in software based redundancy and recovery.

Fernandez calls this “hardware hardening in software.” The idea being that the spare CPU cycles are used to continuously monitor and compare hardware metrics against a state table. If a parameter exceeds the specified threshold, SBC4 will take action to protect itself.

“At a high level, I say, I like to be running at full speed. I can't do that. I'll run at a slower speed. If I can't do that, I'd like to be booted, but not running anything, and then maybe the server will recover. And worst case, I'd like to be powered down rather than get destroyed,” he explained.
At the edge of the edge
FLIP is primarily intended as a proof of concept vehicle, which is to say it’s a test bed for technologies that may eventually find their way to the Moon on other missions.

The inclusion of SBC4 reflects the realities of operating at the far edge of Earth’s orbit. The latency between Earth and the Moon is nowhere near as bad as Mars's up to 44 minute round-trip communication time, but even 2.5 seconds makes real-time control from Houston, or in this case Astrolab’s mission control, which by the way is also powered by HPE's Greenlake Private Cloud stack, in Hawthorne, California a bit unwieldy.

Further complicating matters is the bandwidth afforded the rover. When Artemis 2 traveled around the Moon earlier this year, astronauts weren’t able to send back high-res photographs in real time due to the lack of bandwidth. It was only after the mission was on its way back to Earth that they were able to establish a big enough pipe to transmit the full-res images.
For this reason, SBC4 is designed to operate “at the edge of the edge,” Fernandez said.
Given the bandwidth constraints, it’s far easier to process as much of the data and telemetry gathered by the rover’s array of cameras, lidars, and environmental sensors locally.

“It’s important to ship back insight to Earth rather than all the raw data whenever possible. So having the edge compute capability to process the raw data locally, save on bandwidth back to Earth,” Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews said.

Matthews isn’t the only one to share this perspective. Earlier this year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the challenges and opportunities of space-based computing with analysts during the company’s Q1 earnings call.

"There are many different computing problems that really want to be done in space," he said at the time. "One of the best use cases of GPUs in space is imaging. To be able to do imaging at very large, very high resolutions, extremely large scales and very, very fast, it's hard to do that by sending petabytes and petabytes of imaging data back here on Earth and doing that work, it's easier just to do it out in space."

Though others' ambitions are far greater. Google, Amazon, and SpaceX are all touting orbital datacenters powered by the Sun as the answer to terrestrial power constraints — Elon Musk wants you to believe he'll eventually be manufacturing deep-space datacenters on the Moon and lobbing them into the far reaches of the solar system using mass drivers — the economics of getting those bit barns into low Earth orbit remain unproven and so far unviable.
Despite this, executives and administrators at HPE, Astrolab, Kioxia, and NASA believe that space-based datacenters are still feasible long term.
FLIP
HPE’s Spaceborne Computer 4 will be one of several payloads aboard the FLIP rover.

FLIP will be the largest rover launched by the US since the Apollo program’s manned Moon buggy. And it is by no means small. Designed by Astrolab while measuring roughly 7 feet (2.13 meters) in length and weighing about half a ton, the rover is packed to the gills with cameras, sensors, and even a projector which will eventually be used in place of LCDs on future manned missions to the lunar surface.

For FLIP’s purposes, it’ll mostly be used to project partners' logos onto the Moon’s surface as a sorta advertising gimmick to keep the lights on back at Astrolab’s facilities in Hawthorne while it works on its FLEX rover, which Matthews characterizes as a sort of F150 or Caterpillar tractor for the Moon.

Beyond the scientific equipment, solar panels, and radiators, arguably FLIP’s most striking feature is its disproportionately large wheels. Developed by Venturi Space, along with the rover’s battery pack, these wheels are designed to function much like a pneumatic tire, just without air or rubber. Their size is also intentional. The same wheels found on FLIP are intended for use on NASA’s CLV-1 rover, which is slated to launch in 2028.
Much like FLIP offers HPE as a proving ground to test its lunar compute platform, the rover will do the same for Venturi’s wheels.
Spaceborne Computer 4 and FLIP are slated to launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket later this year and will fly to the Moon’s south pole by Astrobotic’s Griffin-1 lander.

Griffin is classified as a medium class lander measuring roughly 15 feet around and 6.5 feet tall (that’s about 4.5 and 2 meters for those of you living in a nation civilized enough to use metric outside the sciences).

The lander is equipped with seven main engines responsible for everything from trans-lunar injection, trajectory correction, lunar orbit insertion, and powered descent to the surface. Four clusters of attitude control thrusters, meanwhile, will (hopefully) keep the thing pointed the right way up.
FLIP is expected to touch down near the Mons Mouton area along the edge of the South Pole before the end of the year. ®
c2fadc428199286f: A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru.
According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data.

On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server.
"Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF].
ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru.

"ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'."
The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second.

"The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added.

"ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years."

The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory.
The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements.

"Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands.

"The responsibility for these failures did not sit with one organisation alone. ONL created the test account whilst Data Cymru retained overall control of its network, including the ability to instruct ONL to create or remove accounts. Neither had put in place sufficiently clear and effective measures to ensure that old accounts were routinely identified and removed." ®
c7a7043d35fec3f5: WANGARATTA (Australia), Oct 20 — A rural Australian town felt a mix of horror and disbelief today after a highly respected lawmaker was gravely injured in what looked to be a targeted attack.
Former nurse and midwife Helen Haines entered parliament in 2019, earning respect across the political divide for her efforts to stamp out corruption and bolster transparency.
The 65-year-old was struck by a two-tonne SUV in Wangaratta yesterday afternoon, suffering critical injuries in what authorities described as a “deliberate” act of violence.
Wangaratta Mayor Irene Grant said a sombre mood had settled over the town of about 30,000 people, a regional hub about 250 kilometres northeast of state capital Melbourne.
“Helen was well respected. She was diligent and hard working,” Grant told AFP.
“What has happened to Helen has caused the community to step back in utter disbelief. We can’t believe it, people are horrified by what has happened.”
Haines — who lives on a small cattle property outside Wangaratta — was getting something from the trunk of her car when her alleged attacker drove past in a Toyota Land Cruiser.
Authorities said the 43-year-old man turned the car around before veering at Haines and pinning her against her own vehicle.
The driver then allegedly reversed before ramming her again, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
‘Devastated’
Police have said little about the alleged attacker’s motive.
Locals, meanwhile, are struggling to comprehend why anyone would wish harm on the well-liked Haines.
Florist Jess Woodrow said Haines was a friendly face who would pop into the store when she was not tied up in the capital Canberra.
“We are absolutely devastated to hear what has happened. Helen was a beautiful person. She didn’t have a bad bone in her body,” Woodrow told AFP.
“It’s the last thing you would think would happen here.”
Haines entered parliament as an independent lawmaker in 2019, representing the sprawling seat of Indi.
She was a popular representative, holding the seat at the 2025 election with a hefty margin of more than 18,000 votes.
Haines was a vocal champion for greater climate action, better rural healthcare, and help for struggling small businesses.
The First Peoples’ Assembly of Victoria said Haines was a “staunch supporter” of Indigenous rights as well.
But it was her work to hold politicians to account that perhaps earned Haines the most respect both inside and outside parliament.
“Helen Haines is characterised by her kindness, her compassion, her diligence, her intelligence,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.
“She’s someone who is such a strong advocate and is widely respected right across the political spectrum because the way that she advocates is very respectful.” — AFP
f382bc1ee56d8f38: BOGOTÁ, Oct 20 — Ahead of an election that could return the right to power in Brazil, polls show support slipping for recently elected conservative leaders across Latin America.

New surveys in Peru, Colombia, Chile and Argentina suggest voters are losing patience with governments elected on promises to curb crime, revive weak economies and forge closer ties with US President Donald Trump.
Peru’s conservative President Keiko Fujimori and her hardline, gun-toting Colombian counterpart, Abelardo de la Espriella, are the latest newcomers to see their ratings fall.

An Ipsos poll last week showed approval of Fujimori dropping to 40 percent from 57 percent when she took office in August, while De la Espriella’s fell more than three points in his first month in office.

In Chile, where voters elected their most conservative president in three decades last year amid concerns over organized crime, one-quarter of President Jose Antonio Kast’s supporters say they regret backing him, according to the left-wing Fundacion Nodo XXI.
Argentine President Javier Milei, a hero to free-market conservatives across the region, has also seen his ratings hit record lows a year before seeking re-election.

“I think a lot of these governments raised expectations probably unrealistically. People want quick results, which are impossible to produce,” Michael Shifter, senior fellow at The Inter-American Dialogue think tank in Washington, told AFP.
But the backlash has little to do with ideology, he cautioned.
“I’m not sure that if these were governments of the left that it would be any different,” he said.

An AmericasBarometer survey of more than 25,000 people in 21 countries found weak support for the leaders of eight US allies that belong to Trump’s “Shield of the Americas” alliance: Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, Panama and Paraguay.
‘Concrete action’
Nowhere is impatience for better governance more visible than in Bolivia, where voters dumped the long-ruling socialists in the midst of the country’s worst economic crisis in 40 years.
President Rodrigo Paz was elected as a moderate, pro-business alternative, but was only six months into his mandate when demonstrators demanding his resignation blockaded major cities.
Many blame the 59-year-old for failing to end crippling fuel shortages.
“I thought it would be different, that things were going to change,” Jamil Alanoca, a 19-year-old business student, told AFP.
Across the border in Peru, voters went to the polls in April and June seeking relief from an extortion epidemic and are already showing frustration at the lack of results.
“A problem that has persisted for so many years (insecurity) isn’t going to be solved overnight,” Guillermo Loli, director of opinion polls at Ipsos Peru, told AFP.
But “at least concrete actions should be seen,” he said.
The Bukele exception
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s iron-fisted approach to his country’s gangs has earned him a cult-like following.

The self-described “world’s coolest dictator” enjoys approval of 83 percent, according to the AmericasBarometer survey, after driving crime rates to historic lows through a sweeping anti-gang crackdown.
The gains were achieved by jailing more than 90,000 suspects under a four-year-old state of emergency that rights groups say has been marked by serious abuses.

“Bukele’s El Salvador remains a defining experiment — a state that traded liberties for safety and, by these measures, delivered greater safety,” the 2026 Pulse of Democracy report produced by Vanderbilt University using AmericasBarometer polling said.
Shifter expressed doubt that Bukele’s success against domestic gangs could be replicated against the transnational crime networks operating elsewhere in the region.
“Bukele, I think, is really sui generis, he’s the exception,” he said.
Chilean pensioner Leoncio Silva said he believed that, given more time, Kast would vanquish the foreign gangs blamed for a surge in violence in his country.
“Let’s wait a year and see,” he urged. — AFP
0cc474777a4f8856: BARRANQUILLA (Colombia), Oct 20 — Colombia’s new right-wing leader has built himself a costly new presidential palace — a white-columned mansion far from Bogota that doubles as a political manifesto.

Tucked inside a Caribbean military base, President Abelardo de la Espriella’s new headquarters is meant to embody two of his signature promises: a focus on Colombia’s security forces and shifting power away from a capital accused of neglecting the country’s regions.
The austere neoclassical building, set amid tropical gardens and palm trees in Barranquilla, has quickly become one of the most visible symbols of his presidency.
Admirers see a bold statement of decentralisation from a leader determined to govern from beyond Bogota.
“For a very long time, the coast and the regions outside Bogota have been forgotten,” said Libardo Charris, a 54-year-old furniture merchant in Barranquilla.
The debate has even prompted questions about whether a city of about 1.3 million people is the new seat of power.
De la Espriella has frequently refers to Barranquilla as the “alternative capital.”
Critics dismiss it as an expensive political stage set that has earned the mocking nickname “the Temu White House.”

Constitutional experts say transforming Barranquilla into an official alternative seat of government would be difficult, although some Colombian presidents have occasionally governed from cities outside the capital.
“It is not an alternative capital. It is a place where the president stays for a few days and carries out his functions,” constitutional lawyer Juan Manuel Charry told AFP.
Creating a second capital would require constitutional reform and approval by Congress.
Political price tag
From the streets around the sprawling military compound, little of the mansion can be seen.
The property sits inside a restricted area of more than 50,000 square metres, roughly the size of several soccer fields.
A modest sign outside reads: “Presidency of the Republic. Freedom and Order.”
The mansion has already hosted high-profile visitors, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez.
Military personnel continue their daily routines around the complex, while official vehicles, aides and security details come and go.
The facilities include an underground bunker designed to shelter the president and senior civilian and military officials in a crisis.
An admirer of US President Donald Trump, De la Espriella has bristled at comparisons between his new base and the White House.
Yet social media has filled with memes highlighting the resemblance, while critics accuse him of embracing symbolism over substance.
De la Espriella often works from the compound dressed in tactical clothing, dark glasses and a baseball cap, blending into the military surroundings.
He arrives by helicopter or in convoys of armored vehicles, images regularly showcased on his social media accounts.
Recently he led a security operation in a nearby city carrying a pistol on his belt.
Better known as the hometown of pop star Shakira and for its carnival celebrations than as a center of political power, Barranquilla has found itself unexpectedly at the heart of national politics.
Gabriel Sanchez, a 47-year-old shopkeeper, said he welcomed the fact that Colombia’s Caribbean region was now receiving greater attention. Under De la Espriella, he said, the coast is “more visible.”
Street vendor Darlys Patricia Guerrero, 40, said it was “great” to have a presidential headquarters in the sweltering coastal city rather than the high-altitude capital.
“I’ve never seen the president around here,” she told AFP outside the Paradise Battalion base.

At a time of fiscal strain, opponents question the roughly US$650,000 (RM2.7 million) spent renovating the 1938 mansion, according to the Atlantico province’s governor, as well as the cost of moving presidential operations to Colombia’s Caribbean coast.
The criticism is pointed because De la Espriella, a wealthy former lawyer, won office promising a hard line against crime, a defense of traditional values and a leaner state.
Opponents argue that true decentralization requires transferring resources and decision-making powers to the regions rather than relocating the president’s desk.

“There are two governments: the one shown to the cameras and another behind it that we see in the territories,” said Edwin Capaz Lectamo, an Indigenous leader from the southwestern department of Cauca.
Yet beyond the legal questions, political arguments and online jokes, the Barranquilla headquarters has revived a long-running rivalry between Colombia’s Caribbean coast and the Andean capital.
“There’s more joy, more spontaneity here,” said homemaker Alejandra Diaz, 38, comparing her city with Bogota.

Whether it proves a lasting shift in how Colombia is governed or simply a costly symbol, the white-columned mansion has already achieved one thing: turning a building into a national debate about where power belongs. — AFP
