0dbde1ea11534cb3: Despite millions of years of evolution, the development of the human fetus remains a complex process that is vulnerable to genetic, environmental, and metabolic disruptions. These disruptions could result in developmental abnormalities, starting with one of the first organs to begin developing in the fetus that continues to develop after birth: the brain. In a routine prenatal ultrasound, the sonographer will flag possible brain abnormalities for additional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). But imperfect imaging can result in missed or incorrect diagnoses.  To assist with the early detection and treatment of these abnormalities, researchers at MIT, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Inria have developed and trained a deep learning model called E(3)-Pose that helps image the fetus’s head while it’s in motion to capture a high-resolution image that the radiologist can examine. A paper about the work was presented at the 2026 European Conference on Computer Vision.  “One of the problems with having the baby move is that the slices are all over the place,” says first author Ramya Muthukrishnan. Muthukrishnan is an MIT PhD student in the lab of Sunlin (1966) and Priscilla Chou Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Polina Golland, who is a principal investigator at the MIT Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). By slices, Muthukrishnan is referring to a series of 2D images taken during a fetal MRI scan. These 2D planes stacked together effectively make up one high-resolution, 3D image of the fetus’s head. But if the head shifts during imaging, each 2D image “slice” could end up being taken from a different angle, resulting in gaps in the final scan and unusual slice orientation. These problems may cause the physician reviewing the MRI to miss or incorrectly diagnose a pathology in the fetal brain. “There are very fine details that you need a very good volumetric picture of the brain to see,” explains Muthukrishnan. “If you have coverage gaps, you can’t see critical regions, and you need to be able to see well to detect abnormal development.” What makes E(3)-Pose particularly good at tracking fetal motion is its focus on physics. Rather than simply training the model to learn physics from the data, the very principles of physics are baked into the neural network: left-right symmetry of the fetal head is embedded in the model architecture, making it easier for the model to accurately identify the brain’s orientation.  When Muthukrishnan began working on the project at the start of her PhD, she had no background in physics, let alone MRI physics. Most of her experience was in computer science. “I was surprised when I had to go and implement this on the scanner,” she recalls. “I was not prepared for how many times I would crash the scanner because putting things on hardware and getting it to work on hardware is a different beast than training a model to run on data on a GPU.”  Despite the challenges, Muthukrishnan persisted. She remembers shadowing a radiologist who performed fetal MRI scans at Boston Children’s Hospital at the start of her PhD and observing the shared frustration of the patient and radiologist: the pregnant mother felt uncomfortable after spending an hour in an MRI, only to quit the scan halfway; the radiologist was unable to procure a full, high-quality MRI to monitor the development of the fetus. “Seeing frustration about it helped me decide what I wanted to do with my PhD, because it felt like this was a pain point,” Muthukrishnan says. Fortunately, she had help: Co-author Borjan Gagoski, an assistant professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at Boston Children's Hospital, developed a sequence that acquires additional MRI scans to assist with training E(3)-Pose and worked with Muthukrishnan to help troubleshoot the scanner whenever it crashed. Co-author and Boston Children’s Research Assistant Aryn Lee recruited the pregnant volunteers and assisted with acquiring each of the MRI scans. Senior authors who helped guide the project include Elfar Adalsteinsson, MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science; Ellen Grant, the Käthe Beutler Professor of Pediatrics and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School; and Golland. Benjamin Billot, a researcher at Inria and a former postdoc in Golland’s group, helped Muthukrishnan get started with the initial method he developed. “Ramya’s work elegantly combines geometric concepts like equivariance and symmetry with the power of deep learning to change how MRI scanners acquire the images, and to ultimately help the physicians detect and treat problems early in development. It’s an impressive research project that is deep and fundamental in how it models image acquisition, with clear clinical impact,” says Golland. Grant, who directs the Fetal Neonatal Neuroimaging and Developmental Science Center (FNNDSC) at Boston Children’s, adds that Muthukrishnan’s work “will automate fetal brain MRI, replacing today's slow, manual process with faster and more comfortable scans for mothers, while also providing higher-quality images for radiologists to interpret.” E(3)-Pose’s applications could extend beyond motion tracking for fetal MRIs. It could assist with imaging other hard-to-image anatomy, and even autonomous driving applications, where limited sensors need to capture noisy, 3D data in order to track 3D objects. For now, Muthukrishnan hopes to improve E(3)-Pose so that it can help with imaging second-trimester or younger fetuses, as the model is primarily trained on third trimester fetuses. Second-trimester fetuses are “so small, they move around a lot more because there’s more space in the uterus,” Muthukrishnan says. “They’re more important to focus on because the earlier you detect brain abnormalities, the easier it is to intervene.”  This work is supported by the MIT Jameel Clinic, the MIT Takeda Program, the Chou Family Transformative Research Fund, the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering, and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.

141c6aa9e5320924: I went to the iFuture Summit expecting to hear young Malaysians and international graduates ask three prominent panellists—Khairy Jamaluddin, Johor menteri besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi and Selangor menteri besar Amirudin Shari— about jobs, salaries and artificial intelligence.
Instead, one young woman's question stayed with me.
Why should her generation pay for the environmental damage left behind by the generations before them?

Governments celebrate billions of ringgit in investments, she said, but at what cost to the environment? How can future leaders talk about environmental justice while approving developments such as data centres that raise concerns about water consumption, energy use and pollution?
It was a fair question. Why should young people have to grapple with extreme weather and the consequences of decisions they had little say in making?
Khairy challenged young voters to pay closer attention to politicians' environmental commitments.
"My fear is that this issue, when it comes to elections, is quite low down in terms of our priority. Because it's low down in our priority, then the politicians don't act," he said
He is right.

Young people should demand more from their elected representatives when it comes to climate action. But the responsibility for dealing with extreme weather and environmental degradation cannot rest with them alone.
We cannot enjoy decades of development, sometimes fuelled by short-term gains and greed, leave behind the damage, and then expect our children to clean up the mess.
Every time governments announce major investments, we hear plenty about the economic benefits. Far less attention is paid to the environmental trade-offs.
How much water and electricity will these projects consume? What impact will they have on surrounding communities? And who will be held accountable if things go wrong?
These are questions that should be answered before projects receive the green light, not after the damage has been done.
But the environment is not the only issue weighing on the minds of the younger generation.
Uncertain future
There is also AI and the uncertainty it brings to their future careers.
For decades, we have told our children that education is the pathway to opportunity. Study hard, get a degree and build a successful career.
But what happens if the jobs they are preparing for today look very different by the time they graduate?
Amirudin raised concerns about the growing mismatch between university courses and the skills employers need.

That raises another important question: are policymakers giving students and workers a clear picture of where future opportunities lie? And are universities and colleges adapting quickly enough to prepare them for a rapidly changing economy?

As AI reshapes workplaces, young people need more than assurances that new jobs will eventually emerge. They need guidance on the skills they should acquire and a clearer understanding of where demand is headed so they are not constantly playing catch-up.
In many ways, these concerns are connected.
Economic growth, environmental sustainability and employment cannot be discussed in isolation. Decisions made in one area inevitably affect the others.

Listening to the questions raised at the summit, I was struck by how modest the aspirations of many young people actually are. They are not asking for a perfect world. They simply want clean air, safe water and jobs they can rely on in the years ahead.
For decades, we have measured success by how much we build, how much we invest and how quickly the economy grows.
Perhaps it is time to ask a different question, the same one that young woman posed at the summit: what kind of future are we leaving behind for those who will inherit it?
That, surely, is where planning for the future should begin.
The writer is a senior journalist at FMT’s English Desk.
This article represents the writer’s opinion and does not necessarily reflect FMT’s position.
2c76cc087c448162: Hari ini Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim dijadual mempengerusikan apa yang dipanggil mesyuarat Jawatankuasa Peringkat Tertinggi Pengurusan Bencana Pusat. Tidak ada tunggu-tunggu, tidak ada lengah-lengah, tidak ada tidak tahu siapa buat apa. Mesyuarat juga akan membincangkan perkembangan kebakaran di Indonesia. Sekali lagi saya kata obviously. Kebakaran terutama di Kalimantan masih berlaku, malah ada titik panas baharu dikesan.

Lima hari lalu Indonesia meluluskan tawaran bantuan daripada negara jiran bagi menangani kebakaran hutan dan tanah meluas. Dalam bahasa mudah, Indonesia terima bantuan asing tangani kebakaran hutan. Menurut Arrmanatha Christiawan Nasir, si menteri luar Indonesia, Presiden Prabowo Subianto telah meluluskan cadangan bantuan dan kini badan pengurusan bencana nasional mengadakan perbincangan di peringkat teknikal mengenai pelaksanaan. Saya harap perbincangan will not take ages.

Sebelum ini, Prabowo agak keberatan menerima tawaran bantuan negara jiran termasuk Malaysia, dan tidak mahu memberikan status 'bencana negara' ke atas kebakaran di Kalimantan. Begitu juga ketika banjir besar melanda Sumatera, khususnya Aceh tahun lalu. Pelik. Padahal rakyat Indonesia yang menjadi mangsa. Kali ini, seperti di Aceh, ada warga yang meninggal dunia termasuk anggota pasukan pemadam api, dan kesihatan ribuan terjejas akibat haze and smoke-related diseases.

Apa pun, untuk kebakaran di Kalimantan, Malaysia setakat ini menawarkan bantuan pesawat Bombardier, tiga helikopter dan 52 anggota pemadam kebakaran. Di Facebook, saya ada baca 'seruan' rakyat Malaysia berbunyi: "jangan ditolong". I take it yang menyeru demikian tidak mahu negara membantu Indonesia. Jelas ini 'seruan' penuh emosi. Janganlah begitu. Ya, jerebu dari Indonesia tetapi sudah jadi masalah kita. Maksud 'kita' ialah Malaysia, Singapura, Brunei dan tentulah Indonesia sendiri. Sekarang diberitakan jerebu mula merebak ke Jakarta.

Warga Indonesia ramai marah akan pemerintahnya. Sudah ada NGO dan juga individu memfail saman terhadap pemerintah atas dakwaan cuai melampau tangani kebakaran hutan. Yang nyata Indonesia sedang bergelut dengan kebakaran. Lebih 60,000 anggota pemadam api sedang bertungkus-lumus. Tentu ada perkiraannya mengapa Prabowo lambat menyahut tawaran bantuan negara jiran. Wallahu a'lam.

Namun, bantuan negara jiran adalah langkah jangka pendek. The main objective being put out the fires fast. Yang diperlukan juga ialah pelan tindakan jangka panjang dan berterusan kerana jerebu datang setiap tahun. A permanent solution is needed. Now.

Kebakaran berlaku secara terancang. Ia membabitkan hutan tetapi turut terbakar atau dibakar ialah pokok kelapa sawit tua yang buahnya sudah dipungut dan tidak berhasil lagi. Pokok-pokok itu perlu beri laluan untuk penanaman pokok baharu. Membersihkan ladang menggunakan jentera dan segala macam peralatan mengambil masa yang panjang dan menelan kos tinggi. Yes it all about dollars and cents. Maka apilah solusinya bagi syarikat termasuk yang bertaraf 'gergasi' serta tuan punya ladang. Cari mereka yang terlibat dan ambil tindakan? Sudah dibuat dahulu. Jadi mengapa kebakaran berulang saban tahun?
Mungkin tindakan tidak menyeluruh. Mungkin ada syarikat terlepas. Mungkin undang-undang tidak ketat dan denda tidak tinggi. Tidak setimpal dengan apa yang dilakukan. Semuanya kemungkinan.

Kali ini Singapura sudah hantar notis langkah pencegahan kepada tujuh syarikat di Indonesia yang dikaitkan dengan kebakaran hutan dan tanah gambut sehingga menyebabkan jerebu rentas sempadan yang parah. Kata kuncinya ialah 'syarikat di Indonesia'. Oleh itu, mungkin syarikat berpangkalan atau beroperasi di Indonesia tetapi tidak semestinya Indonesian, sebaliknya milik negara asing? Mungkin pemegang konsesi warga Malaysia atau Singapura? 'Syarikat di Indonesia' tentu sahaja boleh juga milik warga Indonesia.

Singapura tidak tolak kemungkinan untuk mengenakan penalti kewangan dan tindakan undang-undang jenayah jika tujuh syarikat yang ia namakan gagal mematuhi notis. Jurucakap Kerajaan Malaysia, Fahmi Fadzil, pula berkata tiada syarikat perladangan Malaysia dikenal pasti terbabit dalam aktiviti pembakaran di Indonesia yang mencetuskan jerebu.
Alhamdulillah, baguslah begitu tetapi 'tiada dikenal pasti' bukan jaminan 100% syarikat kita tidak terbabit. This can only mean they have not been located and identified. I hope this is not the case.

Sama ada syarikat kita terlibat atau tidak, realitinya kita terkesan teruk dengan jerebu. Bak kata Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman, Malaysia mesti bersedia ambil tindakan ke atas syarikatnya jika ada yang terlibat. Beliau mahu bantahan diplomatik Asean diselaraskan serta sekatan pembiayaan terhadap syarikat yang dikaitkan dengan amalan pembakaran terbuka. Kata beliau, bank-bank utama serantau boleh beri tekanan dengan menghentikan pembiayaan kepada syarikat yang didapati terbabit -- syarikat yang walaupun sedikit terkait dengan slash-and-burn tactics ini mesti disekat dan tidak boleh dapat lagi akses modal pasaran dan akses pinjaman, bukan setakat di Malaysia dan Singapura.

Ertinya beliau sarankan cut their access and hurt their wallet. Hurt them where it hurts them most, kata Syed Saddiq. Betul dan mungkin kita akan dapat atasi masalah kebakaran tahunan sekali gus jerebu once and for all.

1246df20968d1512: “Apa khabar?” “Khabar baik.” “Terima kasih.” “Sama-sama.”
These were among the basic Malay exchanges that home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said foreign footballers learnt before their citizenship interviews.

“Adequate knowledge is subjective. Typically, for this category, our practice is that we coach them before the interview: ‘Apa khabar?’ (How are you?), they answer ‘Khabar baik’ (I am well). ‘Terima kasih’ (Thank you), they answer, ‘Sama-sama’ (You are welcome). That is the current practice,” he said.
“It does not say fluent, nor does it require in-depth knowledge. It says adequate. If they understand, we pass them,” he added, according to the New Straits Times.
Saifuddin is defending the level of Malay required by law, but the controversy over the seven players goes well beyond a language test.

Fifa found that falsified documents had been used in the naturalisation and eligibility process, while the Enforcement Agency Integrity Commission (EAIC) uncovered irregularities in the citizenship approvals.
The government must account for how officials handled the applications and assessed the supporting evidence.
Discretion needs limits

Saifuddin has acknowledged that some players did not meet the usual residency period for naturalisation. He argued that the Federal Constitution allowed him to count certain periods spent abroad as residence in Malaysia.
Article 19(3) sets the ordinary requirement at 10 years’ residence within the 12 years before an application, including the 12 months immediately before it.
The EAIC acknowledged the minister’s power to grant special approval under Article 19(2), read with Section 20(1)(e) of Part III of the Second Schedule to the Constitution.
It said the minister considered the players’ potential contribution to Malaysian football when exercising that discretion.
But the power to approve an application does not excuse a failure to follow proper procedures.
The EAIC found that officials considered the special approvals within an extremely short period and in an irregular manner.
It also flagged problems with entry permits, security screening, Malay language assessments and checks on the players’ renunciation of their original citizenship.

The commission urged the home ministry and national registration department (NRD) to review the applications and supporting documents. It also called for clearer guidelines on ministerial discretion and procedures for future cases.
The issue, then, is not simply whether Saifuddin had the power to approve the applications. It is whether officials properly scrutinised them before granting citizenship.
What did the authorities verify?
Saifuddin says the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) must answer for the documents it submitted to Fifa to establish the players’ eligibility to represent Malaysia.
FAM must account for its submissions but its responsibility does not absolve the government of questions about the citizenship process.

Fifa found that falsified documents had been used to claim Malaysian family links for the players. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld the finding of falsification. It restricted the players’ 12-month suspensions to official matches but retained the 350,000 Swiss franc fine against FAM.

The EAIC examined material from both the NRD and FAM and called for a review of the citizenship files. Its public findings do not specify that every document found to be forged went directly to the NRD. The authorities should clarify which documents they received and relied on.
That is central to the case. If doctored documents supported the citizenship applications, how did they pass the authorities’ checks?

The NRD had previously told Fifa that it checked documents relating to the players’ family lineage. Its director-general said officials could not retrieve the original handwritten birth records and issued copies based on secondary evidence.
The department should identify that evidence and explain how officials verified it.
The EAIC also flagged shortcomings in security screening, the Malay language test and checks on renunciation of foreign citizenship.

It noted that requirements concerning the surrender of foreign passports had not been met. As Malaysia does not recognise dual citizenship, the government should explain how officials dealt with these requirements in each case.
CAS did not rule on the legality of the citizenship grants under Malaysian law but that does not make the government’s handling of the applications any less deserving of scrutiny.
The falsification finding and the EAIC’s findings of irregularities demand a proper account of the decisions.
What about other applicants?
The controversy also raises questions about fairness to ordinary citizenship applicants.
Many wait years for a decision. Some have spent most or all of their lives in Malaysia. Their circumstances vary, and not everyone will qualify.
But the government should explain how it applies the law, assesses language proficiency, verifies documents and decides when special approval is justified.
Saifuddin can defend his constitutional powers. He cannot use those powers to sidestep questions about the evidence or the way officials handled the applications.
Nor can the government treat the FAM scandal as a matter for football authorities alone when the citizenship process raises its own concerns.
The language test may be satisfied by a few rehearsed exchanges. The larger test is whether the government can show that officials verified the evidence, followed the rules and applied them properly.
Citizenship is not a favour to be defended after the fact. It is a legal status that demands a credible process.
If the government stands by these approvals, it should produce the evidence that supports them and account for the irregularities the EAIC identified.
Until it does, the questions over how these seven players became Malaysians will remain.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
730492500c4d9ed9: Beberapa hari kini masih lagi terngiang-ngiang soalan berani seorang mahasiswa wanita daripada Universiti Malaya kepada Khairy Jamaluddin dan Onn Hafiz Ghazi, menteri besar Johor. Bagaimanakah seorang yang bergelumang dengan parti seperti Umno dan menjadi figura kontroversial sebagai ketua Pemuda Umno boleh pusing 180 darjah menjadi personaliti yang ada ‘kredibiliti’ di kaca mata semua rakyat termasuk merentas jurang kaum?

That is something incredible yang saya tidak pernah lihat. Berbanding dengan populariti Rafizi Ramli, KJ menang hands down. Soalan kedua saya pula adalah kepada Onn Hafiz. Beliau telah menjawab soalan mahasiswa tersebut dengan suatu syarat iaitu semua pendakwaan rasuah jangan ada sifat pendakwaan terpilih atau selective prosecution. Bukan seperti kes Anwar Ibrahim dulu dengan perubahan tarikh, tempat serta forced confession dua saksi dan macam-macam kerenah yang membuatkan sesiapa mengikuti kes tersebut tidak yakin langsung terhadap pertuduhan dan penghukuman.

Sekarang kita ada RCI Tabung Haji dan pendakwaan pun sedang dijalankan. Kejap nanti kes Felda, Mara dan entah berapa banyak kes lagi. Jelas, dalam pengalaman saya, Melayu yang hendak sokong tidak akan terkata apa-apa secara terbuka sekadar hantar WhatsApp sahaja. Tetapi, Melayu yang tidak bersetuju akan banyak memberi bidasan walaupun tak ada logik dan tak ada perbahasan yang munasabah. Di mana tokoh-tokoh Melayu bukan politik yang bakal menyokong Ummi? Memang tidak akan menjelma dalam kalangan ahli agama, profesor atau tokoh korporat yang berwibawa. She will be alone. Tetapi, kalau ada ahli politik Melayu yang mengecam bukan Melayu, maka ramailah yang akan keluar menjadi hulubalang bangsa. Saya kasihan kepada Ummi yang beranggapan Melayu yang cerdik pandai akan banyak menyokongnya dengan lantang. It will not happen, I am afraid.

Soalan keempat saya adalah implikasi masa depan Melayu. Kita telah melihat kemenangan besar PAS dan Umno di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan. Jangkaan mudah Melaka pun akan dimenangi secara besar oleh PAS dan Umno akan membuktikan penolakan terhadap sindiran Ummi tentang parti politik Melayu dan rasuah. fb34ed50cef3bed0: "From this point forward, all of United States documents and hopefully the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to artificial." That was Donald Trump at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 22, and true to form, he didn't stop at a soundbite.

A week later, he signed an executive order titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence", ordering federal agencies to swap "artificial intelligence" and "AI" for "super intelligence" and "SI" across official documents and websites. The same day, executives from Meta, Nvidia, Google, OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic signed a separate, voluntary White House Accord on Super Intelligence.
It's tempting to laugh this off as branding, especially since Trump's own explanation was that "artificial" "makes intelligence sound fake. It is not fake." But wait a minute.

Words matter, and this one has a specific meaning. The term was popularised by philosopher Nick Bostrom, then at the University of Oxford, in his 2014 book Superintelligence, and it describes not a machine that matches us but one that vastly outperforms the brightest humans in practically every field.

Today's systems aren't there yet, and Trump may simply think "artificial" sounds cheap. But when Meta has had a division literally called Meta Superintelligence Labs since 2025 and the world's most powerful government adopts the same vocabulary, I can't help but feel they are preparing us for something far beyond today's chatbots.
So what does that world look like? Three questions keep nagging at me.
Do we still need schools?

Six years ago, I argued in this column that AI could help fix our broken school system, pointing to Chinese and American platforms that taught maths at each student's own pace. The evidence has since piled up faster than I expected.

In 2025, the World Bank published the results of a six-week after-school programme in Nigeria's Edo State, where students worked in pairs with Microsoft Copilot, a GPT-4-powered assistant, in up to two 90-minute sessions a week under a teacher's supervision. The gains, the lead researchers later wrote, "correspond to nearly 1.5 years of typical learning in just six weeks", outperforming around 80% of the education programmes tested in randomised trials across the developing world.

Now imagine that this tutor isn't merely good but superintelligent and available to every child in every kampung at any hour. The classroom as a place where a teacher pours the same facts into a roomful of young heads at the same speed and we simply can't compete with that.

But schools will survive, because they'll become the place where children learn what no machine can learn on their behalf: how to make friends, lose gracefully, argue without hating and work alongside people who aren't like them. As I wrote back then, the secret ingredient is EQ, or emotional intelligence, and a superintelligent tutor only makes it more precious.
Why would we even work?

In 1930, the British economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that within a century we would be so much richer that "three-hour shifts or a fifteen-hour week" might be all the work we would need. We are four years from his deadline, and Malaysian law still sets the normal working week at up to 45 hours, three times what he imagined.

Elon Musk, never one for understatement, thinks the machines will finally deliver on that promise. "In a benign scenario, probably none of us will have a job," he told the VivaTech conference in Paris in 2024, with what he called "universal high income" taking the place of wages.
I'm not going to pretend that's guaranteed, since whether superintelligence brings abundance for all or riches for a few depends on who owns the machines.

But if we get it right, Keynes already told us what our real challenge would be: "how to use his freedom from pressing economic cares, how to occupy the leisure, which science and compound interest did for him, to live wisely and agreeably and well." Work won't vanish so much as become something we choose, like a Sunday evening game of futsal.
What does a world of superintelligent humanoids look like?
Years ago, I toured a factory outside Shenzhen that was frantic with activity yet almost void of human life. Those were single-purpose machines, impressive but hardly intelligent.

Today's humanoids are something else entirely. In July 2025, China's Unitree priced its R1 humanoid at 39,900 yuan, about RM24,000, while Musk has said Tesla's Optimus could eventually cost RM82,000 to RM123,000 once it's mass-produced.

Investment bank Morgan Stanley expects close to a billion humanoids in use by 2050, mostly in industry and commerce. Put a superintelligent mind inside each of those bodies and the list of "AI-proof" jobs I published in this column in 2020, from construction worker and mechanic to nurse and caregiver, goes straight into the bin.

Picture a machine that harvests paddy in Kedah at dawn, rewires your house by noon and sits with your ageing parents through the night, never tired and never impatient. That isn't a dystopia. It's the end of drudgery.

Whatever Trump's reasons for choosing the name, the industry he's naming has made no secret of where it's heading. Keynes addressed his essay to "our grandchildren" - the generation that would first have to decide what to do with all that freedom, and it turns out those grandchildren are us – or at least the younger ones among us.

631c78f18e2760a2: In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them the perfect material for the job. Unfortunately, that approach doesn’t work well yet, and the problem comes down to data: Most materials consist of 3D arrangements of crystals, not the text streams that today’s large language models are trained on. The experimental literature is also heavily biased toward a few popular classes of crystals, making AI outputs skew toward those materials. Now MIT researchers have created a multimodal AI model that tackles these problems. The model combines 3D atomic structures with natural language descriptions to create rich linguistic descriptions about the structures from experimental research papers and first-principles computational databases. The unified description outlines not just the chemical composition and structure, but also its properties, processing considerations, and potential applications, helping AI learn more about what makes materials impactful. In a new paper in Nature Communications, the researchers showed their system could identify better material designs than models trained on text streams alone by allowing the model to “see” the atomic arrangements and bonding patterns. For example, when the researchers asked the model to identify materials suited for solid-state lithium-ion battery electrolytes, its top results included materials that had been independently identified as promising candidates. The researchers also showed their model learned geometric representations of material structures in ways text-only models could not. “Structure is really at the heart of the materials science field,” says Ju Li, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor in Power Engineering in the departments of Materials Science and Engineering and Nuclear Science and Engineering. “If you understand the structure, you can infer quite a lot about the properties and performance of materials. We wanted to build the connection between a material’s atomic structure and its properties and processing for the model.” Joining Li on a paper about the model are Yang Jeong Park, first author and former MIT postdoc; Mayank Kumaran, a recent University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign computer engineering graduate; Chia-Wei Hsu SM ’26; and Elsa Olivetti, the Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor in Engineering in DMSE. Getting models to see in 3D Materials scientists are always on the hunt for new crystals that will lead to the products of the future. Over the last decade, AI has reshaped that process, proposing and designing new crystalline structures, which have highly ordered atomic structures and make up more than 90 percent of solid materials on Earth. Most of those models treat solid crystalline materials as 3D graphs. The rise of large language models has given researchers another tool for innovation. But existing large language models rely heavily on text from published papers and books, limiting their knowledge of the physical world, since many potential crystal structures are stored in computational databases. Text-based models also lack understanding of visual geometry. To overcome those challenges, the researchers decided to create a vision-language model for crystalline materials. They trained a language model to create textual descriptions of crystal structures using an approach known as contrastive learning, in which models compare similar and dissimilar examples of structures and textual descriptions to achieve a unified understanding. This is similar to aligning the visual and language regions of the brain. Following training, the researchers compared the predictions of two versions of the model: one trained on a dataset containing the AI-generated descriptions and the other trained on a dataset containing text from papers only. They found that the model trained on AI-generated descriptions successfully learned how to align geometric structures with text descriptions while the other did not. “We wanted to create an AI model that works broadly across materials,” Li says. “That’s why we decided to synthesize narratives rather than rely solely on existing papers. We found when we used that narrative dataset, the models are better at predicting the function.” Accelerating materials science The researchers then showed their model could be given a natural language query describing a property and identify crystalline materials with that property, outperforming a baseline. “There are sometimes these step changes within materials science around algorithmic integration toward useful tools, which the community uses to further advance the field,” Olivetti says. “This approach helps us see more deeply into three-dimensional structures and link structures to property and processing. I hope this can be one of those step changes.” Li compares the model to AlphaFold, an AI model that links protein structures with function that has helped advance biological research and drug development. The researchers believe their new approach can work with many crystalline materials, and they hope other material scientists will use it to accelerate their work. “Being able to see a three-dimensional crystal and how its atoms are connected is super foundational,” Li says. “I think this will be useful to anyone who practices materials science.” The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Defense Threat Reduction Agency through the University Research Alliance; the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; and the National Research Foundation of Korea.

4a57d3c28cf22595: I’m not shocked by the revelation that some children are refusing to sit next to their Christian or Muslim classmates. I knew it was coming.
On Oct 15, Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin raised concerns in the Dewan Rakyat about religious intolerance among primary school children.
He said a teacher told him that some children said: “I don’t want to sit with them because they eat pork,” or “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross”.

This is far more than a classroom management problem. It is a symptom of a society that is quietly fracturing along ethnic and religious lines — and in Malaysia’s multiethnic reality, that fracture is a national security threat.

In a country where the delicate balance between the Malay-Muslim majority and the Chinese, Indian, and indigenous minorities has historically been the cornerstone of stability, the early crystallisation of “us versus them” at the primary-school level is terribly dangerous, to say the least.

When children are socialised to view difference as a threat rather than a shared reality, the foundation of our society — the mutual accommodation that has kept us together for decades — begins to crumble before critical thinking even develops.
As Mongin warned, if this trend is not addressed at the youngest age, it will inevitably spread, feeding the very 3R controversies that have destabilised Malaysian politics in recent years.
This should not be treated as an isolated case for it reflects deeper structural patterns that threaten Malaysia’s unity.

It is dangerous because it erodes the trust and understanding that underpin social relations, business partnerships and even political alliances. Worse, it creates a radicalisation pipeline: isolated children become vulnerable to extremist online narratives.
I said I knew it was coming. The rise of ethno-religious nationalism, especially since the early 2000s, has amplified our differences.

When an increasing number of politicians unashamedly fire up religion- or race-related issues to win votes or to be seen as champions of their race or religion — and then get away with it or are cheered on by their supporters — what do you expect to happen?
Political rhetoric often frames racial and religious purity as mobilisation tools, and children absorb the tone of such public discourse.
Another reason is that the different communities have moved into their own silos, interacting at work, in school and elsewhere only when and where necessary.

And unlike in the past, the norm today is for children to play or share activities with those of their own race. When school is the only mixed space, and that space is already poisoned by home prejudices or online content, the classroom turns into a battleground instead of a bridge.

Digital poisoning makes the problem worse. Some social media platforms prioritise outrage, with algorithms amplifying hate speech and fake news. Children encounter dehumanising content that normalises rejection of the “other.”
When a pupil says, “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross,” they may have internalised a viral meme or attack on that symbol.
I can go on, but all of us know there are many unspeakable elephants in the room that authorities need to address.
Existing “unity” programmes are well-intentioned but episodic and top-down. They rely on short camps or lectures rather than daily, sustained interaction.

Without structural changes in curriculum and teacher training, they will continue to fail in shifting deep prejudices. Teacher training must include conflict resolution and intercultural communication. Remedies must be structural, not performative as they have been.

Curriculum reform should prioritise critical thinking, media literacy and emotional intelligence over rote “unity” modules. Students need to learn how to deconstruct hate speech and engage in dialogue.
Schools need more group activities to build positive associations.
Digital literacy must become a core subject, not an add-on. Perhaps workshops can be organised for parents on how to guide their children’s online consumption.
Government and civil society must emphasize shared third spaces — mixed sports leagues, arts programmes and community projects — to generate organic positive interactions.
Above all, political leaders must stop exploiting religious and racial divisions for gain. Rhetoric that validates children’s prejudices undermines the very unity they are supposed to defend.

The refusal by six-year-olds to share a desk is small in scale but carries enormous weight. It is a snapshot of Malaysia at a crossroads. If treated as a minor issue, the country risks losing its social cohesion entirely.
If addressed with serious, structural reforms in education, digital literacy and political leadership, genuine unity may be possible.

In a multiethnic society, separation is not merely a social preference — it is a national security threat. Malaysia cannot afford to let its youngest generation grow up believing that difference is a threat rather than a shared reality. The time for action is now.

9fd1af01b713f727: From Moaz Nair

In the noble effort to elevate Bahasa Melayu as the core of national identity, a topic frequently discussed among language enthusiasts is the level of mastery and fluency of the national language among multi-ethnic communities.
Most narratives typically focus on daily communication, the corporate sector, or administrative affairs.

However, from a sociolinguistic perspective, there is a dimension that is rarely explored deeply but carries significant influence over language assimilation: the use of the national language within the religious and cultural expressions of non-Muslim communities.
On one hand, there are high expectations for all citizens to anchor their lives around Bahasa Melayu. On the other, when touching upon the spiritual realm, a more complex dynamic emerges.

Understanding these contrasting approaches is not meant to assign blame, but rather to examine how language can function more inclusively as a bridge for unity without disrupting established socio-religious sensitivities.
Historical framework and the unique situation in the peninsula

The difficulty of expanding the use of Bahasa Melayu in non-Muslim religious affairs in Peninsular Malaysia is rooted in a combination of legal history, demographics, and the evolution of the language's corpus itself.

Under Article 160 of the Federal Constitution, Malay identity is clearly defined by three main elements: professing the religion of Islam, habitually speaking the Malay language, and conforming to Malay custom. This close alignment has caused Bahasa Melayu to evolve with a heavy Islamic imprint over hundreds of years through the absorption of Arabic theological terms into everyday vocabulary.

To preserve harmony and prevent theological confusion, most states in the peninsula enforce the Enactment on the Control and Restriction of the Propagation of Non-Islamic Religions, guided by the principles of Article 11(4) of the Federal Constitution. These laws restrict the use of certain religious terms to ensure the doctrinal integrity of the majority community remains protected.
Aware of these legal and social sensitivities, non-Muslim communities in the Peninsula—comprising largely Chinese and Indian ethnic groups—opt for a cautious approach.

To maintain racial harmony and safeguard their respective theological purity, they feel more comfortable retaining their mother tongues (such as Mandarin or Tamil) or English in their religious affairs. This situation inadvertently creates a linguistic divide in spiritual matters, even though they are fluent in Bahasa Melayu in other daily affairs.
Diverse models in East Malaysia and Indonesia

The reality in the peninsula presents a stark contrast when looking at the socio-political models in Sabah, Sarawak, and Indonesia. In East Malaysia, a unique demographic structure has long positioned Bahasa Melayu as the primary unifying vessel.

For hundreds of indigenous sub-ethnicities such as the Iban, Kadazandusun and Bidayuh, Bahasa Melayu has served as the daily lingua franca, including in church services and their Alkitab (Bible) texts.

The general practice and sharing of religious terms rooted in the same language are accepted with high tolerance as a historical norm, in line with the socio-political guarantees under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63).

Looking at our neighbour, Indonesia underwent a comprehensive language assimilation process because Bahasa Indonesia was established as a neutral and inclusive national asset. There, all recognised religions fully utilise Bahasa Indonesia in rituals and scripture translations.
Major Islamic figures and organisations like Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) and Muhammadiyah play a mature role in guiding society.
They have successfully educated the public by decoupling the language’s function as a national communication tool from the essence of an individual's personal faith.
This approach allows for the harmonious sharing of certain religious vocabularies, anchored by the concept of inter-citizen brotherhood or “ukhuwah wathaniyah”.
Building harmony through mutual understanding
These differing linguistic approaches have a tangible impact on daily social relations. In the peninsula, the separation of language in religious affairs shapes a model of "cautious coexistence".

Multi-ethnic communities deeply respect each other’s boundaries, yet opportunities for deeper cross-cultural dialogue can sometimes be limited by fears of stepping on legal sensitivities. Social interactions remain largely concentrated in secular spaces like economics, education and sports.

Conversely, the dynamics in Sabah, Sarawak and Indonesia demonstrate that when a national language is shared in the most deeply personal aspect of life—spirituality—it can erode suspicion and strengthen a sense of togetherness. The national language is no longer seen as the exclusive property of one group, but as a grand canopy sheltering all citizens.
Conclusion
The desire to see Bahasa Melayu fully embraced by all Malaysians is a noble dream that deserves support. However, discourses on elevating the language must look beyond casual conversation.

We must acknowledge the sociolinguistic challenge that arises when the national language is restricted in non-Muslim spiritual realms to safeguard faith, while simultaneously expecting these communities to assimilate the language into every facet of their lives.

To move forward, the best path is to construct a harmonious, localised understanding. Drawing from the spirit of tolerance in East Malaysia, we can begin to view Bahasa Melayu not as a tool of division, but as a bridge that unites.

Without compromising the legal protections that safeguard the faith of Muslims in the peninsula, the cultivation of the national language in cultural and literary spaces across all communities must continue to be nurtured maturely—for the future of a truly integrated Bangsa Malaysia.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

c46893703f4038fb: There is something curious about the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) being shortlisted for the Asian Football Confederation’s (AFC) Member Association of the Year (Gold) award.

Malaysian football has spent months grappling with questions about governance, eligibility and accountability. Now its governing body is in the running for one of the region’s top administrative honours.
The winner will be announced at the AFC’s awards ceremony in Bangkok on Nov 19. FAM shares the shortlist with the FA of Hong Kong, China Limited, and the All India Football Federation.
Perhaps FAM has done enough in certain areas to merit consideration. But what exactly does the AFC reward when it names a member association of the year?
A trophy can recognise activity. It should not substitute for scrutiny of the institution behind it.

AFC general secretary Windsor John says associations submit reports on their activities and programmes. A selection panel awards points for areas such as grassroots development, youth competitions and hosting, with three associations shortlisted in each category.
Asked how the assessment treats governance and accountability, and whether strong programme delivery can offset institutional weaknesses, Windsor said:
“The assessment takes into account a wide range of areas of football in an association. You score high in some, medium in some and probably no score in other areas.”

His answer suggests that the panel assesses associations across several areas, with varying scores. But it does not explain how much weight governance carries, or whether strong results in some categories can compensate for serious weaknesses in others.
That is a fair question about an award meant to recognise an association as a whole. It does not mean the AFC ignored governance when assessing FAM.
The criteria and their weightings should make clear how institutional accountability is judged.
For FAM, the timing makes that scrutiny unavoidable.

The naturalisation scandal has damaged confidence in Malaysian football. Fifa’s sanctions over the eligibility case exposed serious failures that the national association could not brush aside with promises to move on.
The affair raised questions not only about player eligibility, but also about the controls and oversight expected of the body responsible for the national game.

September’s extraordinary congress brought another test. The Football Association of Selangor (FAS) had objected to the eligibility of the electoral committee chairman, a concern also raised by Windsor.

FAM’s electoral code, endorsed at its June 4 congress, states that the chairperson and deputy chairperson of the electoral committee must be qualified to practise law. Yet the congress proceeded amid questions over whether the committee met that requirement.
Electoral rules protect the legitimacy of the process and the people it puts in office. An association that revises its rules must follow them, even when compliance creates an inconvenient problem.
FAM cannot demand respect for its authority while treating its own rules as obstacles to negotiate away.
Governance as part of the scorecard
There is also the AFC’s audit of FAM, which many have urged the association to release in full.

Only part of the report had been presented at the extraordinary congress in June and critics argued that the public deserved to know the full findings, warning that withholding them could fuel speculation.
Prepared by AFC deputy secretary-general Vahid Kardany, the report highlighted weaknesses in governance, accountability and organisational management.
It found that FAM’s administrative structure had not received formal executive committee approval.
It also pointed to decision-making concentrated around certain individuals and critical functions heavily dependent on them.
Weak systems for retaining institutional knowledge threatened continuity and could discourage staff from raising concerns.
These are not cosmetic flaws. A sports association needs clear lines of responsibility, systems that survive leadership changes and an environment where staff can report problems without fear.
Otherwise, the institution risks becoming dependent on a handful of people rather than sound processes.
Football development raises another pressing question.

Malaysia’s U-23, U-19 and U-16 teams have struggled to remain competitive in Asean and reach the Asian stage. Their results demand scrutiny of the system meant to prepare young Malaysians for international football.
The National Football Development Programme (NFDP) was designed to produce a technically superior generation by 2025.
Yet questions persist about its outcomes, coaching standards, talent identification and the number of players progressing to senior international football.
Malaysia has repeatedly reworked its structures while regional rivals continue to develop their talent pools. Academies, coaches and thousands of trainees are not proof of success by themselves.
How many players become professionals? How many earn senior international caps? How many fulfil the promise that justified the investment?
FAM has taken on a greater role in NFDP’s technical implementation. It now has an opportunity to show what a more focused system can deliver.
Another revamp, however, is not an achievement in itself. Results must follow.
The Malaysian Football League’s problems add to the wider unease. Salary arrears and Fifa sanctions involving clubs expose persistent weaknesses in the domestic game.

FAM and the MFL are separate bodies, so responsibility for individual cases must be established rather than casually assigned to the national association. Still, activity reports alone cannot capture the health of Malaysian football.
The AFC may have sound reasons for shortlisting FAM. The nomination does not prove the panel got it wrong, nor does it mean FAM has achieved nothing worthy of recognition.

But an award bearing the title Member Association of the Year suggests more than a tally of activities. If the AFC wants the honour to command respect, it should explain how its criteria assess both an association’s output and the way it governs itself.
FAM, too, should welcome scrutiny rather than hide behind the nomination. Recognition will mean little while questions about its elections, audit findings and development record remain unanswered.
A trophy can decorate a cabinet, but it cannot repair a governing system, develop a generation of footballers or restore public confidence.
Before anyone celebrates the award, the more important question is whether the association has done the work to earn the trust that the honour is supposed to represent.

1fb61941d5b43ee1: From Jason Chuah
Malaysia has staked a good deal of its economic future on a few dozen strands of fibre lying on the seabed.

More than 20 international submarine cables land at over 10 stations in this country, and with its digital economy blueprint the government aims to make Malaysia Southeast Asia’s leading destination for cable landings.
They carry almost all of our international data, including the traffic behind Johor’s data-centre boom. Yet the criminal law that protects them was written for the telegraph.

The only provision aimed squarely at cable damage is Section 431A of the Penal Code. It punishes mischief by cutting or injuring “any electric telegraph cable, wire, line, post, instrument or apparatus for signalling”, with up to two years imprisonment or a fine.
The provision has three serious weaknesses.
First, it requires mischief, meaning intention or knowledge that loss or damage is likely.
A ship that drags its anchor across a cable through carelessness might well fall outside it, and so does one that merely claims carelessness.
That is exactly the explanation offered in almost every recent incident, from the Baltic Sea to the Taiwan Strait. Proving mischief will not be easy.
Second, it stops at the territorial sea. The Penal Code applies to offences committed “within Malaysia”, which takes in our 12-nautical-mile territorial waters but no more.
Its extraterritorial provisions reach Malaysian citizens and Malaysian-registered ships, but not a foreign crew aboard a foreign vessel.
Most of a cable’s route lies further out, in the exclusive economic zone and on the continental shelf.
The Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1984 and the Continental Shelf Act 1966 regulate the laying of cables but do not make damaging them an offence.
A foreign ship that cuts a cable 30 miles off our coast commits, so far as Malaysian criminal law is concerned, no offence at all.

Third, the language is out of date. Modern fibre-optic cables probably count as “apparatus for signalling”. The planned subsea power link carrying a gigawatt of Sarawak’s electricity to Singapore almost certainly does not.

International law regrettably does not fill the gap. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which Malaysia ratified in 1996, is better at protecting the freedom to lay cables than the cables themselves.

Article 113 obliges states to criminalise the wilful or culpably negligent breaking of cables, but only by ships flying their own flags and their own nationals. Malaysia’s law, which ignores negligence, arguably does not meet that obligation.
Worse, Article 97 says that when an “incident of navigation” occurs beyond the territorial sea, only the flag state may prosecute the master or crew.

Nor does it give any right to board a ship suspected of damaging a cable. So when a vessel flying a flag of convenience drags its anchor through a cable in our EEZ, UNCLOS refers us to a flag state that has neither the means nor the will to act.

This is not hypothetical. In May, the director-general of the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency acknowledged that tankers carrying Iranian-linked oil choose to transfer cargo about 70km off Johor precisely to “exploit jurisdictional gaps”.
One monitoring group counted 42 such transfers there in about 10 weeks. They operate in the very waters where Malaysia’s criminal law stops.
The United Kingdom faced the same problem and offers a useful model. Its principal offence dates from 1885 but was long ago extended to the continental shelf.
In May 2026 the British government went further, announcing a new criminal framework covering damage that is intentional or reckless, with tougher penalties.
Malaysia should do three things.
First, replace section 431A with a dedicated offence covering intentional, reckless and culpably negligent damage to telecommunications and power cables, with penalties that reflect what is at stake.
Second, extend that offence expressly to the EEZ and continental shelf, applying to any person, whatever their nationality or flag.
Third, draft it with the enforcement problem in mind.
In August 2026 the Helsinki Court of Appeal revived the prosecution of the crew of the Eagle S, a shadow-fleet tanker accused of cutting cables in the Gulf of Finland.

The court held that the offence was committed where its effects were felt, in Finland. It also held that deliberate anchor-dragging is not a mere “incident of navigation” that UNCLOS reserves to the flag state.

The coastal state suffering the cable damage can therefore have criminal jurisdiction. A Malaysian statute that locates the offence where the damage is suffered, and defines it accordingly, would put our courts on the same footing.
Malaysia, which has long taken a robust view of coastal-state rights, is better placed than the great maritime powers to take this step. What it lacks is a law fit for the age of fibre.
Jason Chuah is chairman of the Board of Research at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia and an FMT reader.

d9ad1ab514e787dd: From P Kamalanathan
Last week, a young student at AIMST University asked me: “Datuk, did Rajinikanth go to university?”
I smiled.
Rajini studied in a Kannada-medium school and worked as a coolie, carpenter and bus conductor in Bangalore.
He joined a film institute at 25, an age when we tell our youth, “You are late.”
Last week, Jailer 2 was breaking box-office records again. At 74, he is still a superstar.
We celebrate his punchlines, but we ignore his lessons on education.
As a former deputy minister of education who oversaw five million students, I see five lessons from Rajini that our new National Education Plan 2026-2035 is trying to teach.
First: Learning agility beats certificates
Rajini had no degree. But he had what the ministry now calls “learning agility”. From stage plays to learning Hindi for Andha Kanoon to learning motion capture for Enthiran, he never stopped.
In Switzerland this year, I saw Swiss CEOs with no MBAs but 10 micro-credentials in AI. That is the Rajini model: lifelong TVET.
Second: Discipline is education
Director SP Muthuraman once said that Rajini was the first to arrive and the last to leave. In 50 years, there has been no “Rajini late” headline.
We chase tuition, but our students fail because they cannot wake up at 6am. Discipline, like that of the Bangalore bus conductor punching tickets at 5am, is the first certificate.
Third: Humility is Karamah Insaniah
The National Education Plan speaks of Karamah Insaniah, or the recognition and uplifting of human dignity. Look at Rajini.
He is a superstar, yet he sits on the floor, touches elders' feet and says, “I am a small child of K Balachander.”
In an age of TikTok arrogance, he teaches adab. My mother always taught me that education without humility is noise.
Fourth: Reinvention in the AI age

Rajini, at 74, is learning AI filmmaking for Jailer 2. If a 74-year-old can act with de-ageing technology, our youth can earn Google AI certification, which the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) offers free in Selangor.
Fifth: Do well, do good

Rajini famously said, “Money comes, goes. Give.” He built schools quietly. This is what I tell my colleagues at the Public Relations Practitioners Society of Malaysia: sustainability is a competitive advantage. Rajini has sustained a 50-year career because people trust his goodness.
That student asked if Rajini passed his exams. I told him: He did not pass with straight As, but he passed the hardest exam: life.
This Deepavali, when we watch Rajini on screen, let us tell our children:
Don’t copy his style; copy his discipline.
Don’t just whistle for the superstar; learn to be a superstar in your own trade, whether as a welder, coder or teacher.
Because, as Rajini said in Padayappa: “En vazhi, thani vazhi”, or “My way is my own way”.
Let our education system allow every Malaysian child to find their own way.
P Kamalanathan is an MIC central working committee member and a former deputy education minister.

814a9ce3b76d1166: Apabila sesebuah kerajaan Malaysia memasuki tahun ketiga pemerintahan dan membentangkan belanjawan untuk tahun berikutnya, ada satu soalan yang lazim ditanya, apatah lagi jika belanjawan menawarkan pelbagai inisiatif yang dilihat baik untuk rakyat. Yang bertanya termasuklah ahli politik terutamanya pembangkang, penganalisis dan ahli akademik, media, dan orang ramai.
Pertanyaannya ialah, adakah belanjawan yang dibentang satu belanjawan pilihan raya? Mengapa ditanya sedemikian ialah kerana banyak goodies yang diberi menerusi belanjawan itu.

Most of the time yang diluah bukan pertanyaan. Sebaliknya, ia satu syak oleh orang yang bertanya. Si penanya sudah membuat kesimpulan sendiri sebelum bertanya, hence giving a statement under the guise of a question. Lalu orang yang bertanya mensyaki goodies bertujuan untuk mengambil hati rakyat supaya mengundi parti memerintah yakni pihak yang membentangkan belanjawan apabila pilihan raya diadakan kelak.
Adakala apa yang disyaki memang benar. Adakala tidak. Boleh dikata semua kerajaan pernah menghadapi persoalan seumpama itu.

Tempoh hari Anwar Ibrahim membentangkan belanjawan untuk 2027. Like PMX or not kena akui it is a good budget. Banyak memberi manfaat kepada pelbagai lapisan rakyat sekali gus menimbulkan 'syak' this is an election budget. Sebenarnya sebelum Anwar bentang belanjawan pun, ada pihak sudah kata apa yang akan dibentang ialah belanjawan pilihan raya meskipun mandat kerajaan akan hanya tamat pada Februari 2028.

Semasa belanjawan dibahaskan di Parlimen, ada yang timbulkan soal election budget. Ketua Pembangkang Hamzah Zainudin mendakwa belanjawan kali ini sarat dengan pengumuman berbentuk apa yang beliau sifatkan 'gula-gula'. Kata beliau, "banyak manis-manis mungkin pilihan raya tahun depan".

Berkata begitu boleh dilihat Hamzah menjangkakan rakyat akan termakan 'gula-gula'. Mungkin Hamzah bimbang 'gula-gula' akan memberikan kesan negatif ke atas pembangkang apatah lagi apabila ada pemimpin kanan PAS menyambut baik belanjawan itu. Lalu Hamzah mendakwa bantuan atau 'gula-gula' bukan faktor penentu undi.

Kata-kata itu meskipun boleh dilihat sebagai perli dan menyerang kerajaan, mungkin juga disuarakan untuk menenangkan pembangkang, jika mereka sudah cemas. Juga menaikkan semangat untuk melawan. Pendapat saya mudah: Tak kisahlah bajet pilihan raya atau bukan, janji rakyat dapat manfaat.

Lantas saya setuju dengan pandangan kawan lama saya, Kassim Muhamad, bahawa gagasan ekonomi tidak semestinya kedengaran berdegum-degum. Belanjawan yang manusiawi juga gagasan ekonomi kerana ia melibatkan orang biasa.

"Bagi sesetengah orang gagasan ekonomi mestilah kedengaran gah dan besar biar berdegum. Bagi orang biasa seperti saya, nasib orang biasa yang bergelut mencari sesuap nasi, segala bentuk bantuan itu sangat bermakna," kata si kawan lama.

Kassim memberi contoh: Bantuan kepada pesara RM750. "Ini bukanlah bentuk gagasan berdegum. Orang boleh saja melabelnya gula-gula. Seperti juga hasrat supaya warung di bandar kita diberi perhatian juga tidak gah tetapi jelas aspek sifat manusiawinya."
Bagi beliau ini bukan belanjawan pilihan raya. Ia bajet yang punya sifat manusiawi. Ini elemen penting walau apa pun bajet itu digelar.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
e3450c0821b6e75b: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim likes to quote renowned thinkers in his speeches. Critics have said he likes to parade his erudition, which they argue is pointless because he fails to follow through with implementation.

In his budget speech the other day, he cited Isaiah Berlin, the Latvia-born and English-naturalised philosopher, famed for inventing the “hedgehog and the fox” metaphor in a celebrated essay on Leo Tolstoy’s meditation on history.

Berlin divided history’s seminal thinkers into hedgehogs and foxes: hedgehogs being those who relate everything to a central vision (Marx, Nietzsche); while foxes (Shakespeare, Montaigne, Sophocles) pursue multiform, even contradictory, insights to their finale.
He held that Tolstoy was a fox, a brilliant discerner of particularities, who towards the end of his life flirted with disaster by trying to be a hedgehog.

The metaphor sheds light on the concerns raised by Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin about schoolchildren refusing to sit next to classmates because they eat prohibited foods or wear religious symbols of other faiths.
Willie did not say from where the aversion stemmed but few would have difficulty in knowing the motivation.

Interestingly, the problem of polarisation among school pupils can be helped by understanding Berlin’s musings. He said that human beings have to be both hedgehogs and foxes; we maim our sensibility if we choose the exclusivity of the one and dissolve into nihilism if, fox-like, we opt for contradictions that lead nowhere.
Willie has highlighted a problem during the tenure of a prime minister who, in his youth, championed a cause that has contributed to the dilemma facing our education system.
Fortunately, the same leader has access to the ideas needed to free those trapped by a form of exclusivity that harms. He is aware of the way out. Would that he opted for it.
Our children should be open to being both hedgehog and fox.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
4d556263d22f1c96: The prime minister’s announcement that the government will phase out the contract system for medical officers and offer permanent posts to more than 9,000 contract doctors in 2027 has injected some hope into the healthcare workforce.
Budget 2027 also raised the post-basic incentive for nurses and paramedics from RM100 to RM200 a month, and the Air Health Service incentive from RM30 to RM100.
These moves recognise that a health service cannot run on buildings and equipment alone. It depends on people who are trained, supported and willing to stay.

These are significant commitments. However, success will ultimately depend on whether the government can recruit these healthcare workers, relocate them and provide the support they need to remain where their services are most needed.
Recent figures show why the situation remains troubling.
In the latest round of medical officer postings, only 673 of the 1,055 medical officers offered placements in Sabah and Sarawak had reported for duty.
Those who did not report cited relocation costs, personal and family circumstances, health concerns and limited opportunities for specialist training.

In all fairness, the health ministry has made significant strides over the past few weeks in addressing these concerns and taking immediate steps to retain healthcare workers, particularly young medical officers.

For doctors moving to East Malaysia, the government had already agreed in February to allow eligible contract doctors offered permanent appointments in 2025 to claim transfer and relocation costs, with claims of up to 100% for inter-regional moves.
Earlier this month, the ministry also confirmed approval for claims by specified cohorts.
This represents significant progress, but it is important to clarify that this is not a newly introduced allowance.
On social media, officers continue to express frustration over the lack of clarity and transparency in the application and payment processes.

Clear rules on eligible expenses, advances, documentation and payment timelines are needed. Most importantly, these rules must be communicated to relocating officers in a timely manner so they can access the support before relocation costs become a barrier.
Additionally, on Oct 8, the health minister said that eligible medical officers returning to their home regions could receive a disturbance allowance equivalent to one month’s basic salary.

Later that week, the minister also announced that the ministry was studying a proposal to allocate a dedicated 30% share of Federal Training Award places to medical officers serving in Sabah and Sarawak. Both measures could make postings more attractive, but the proposed training quota remains under study and has yet to be implemented.
For those who are unclear about the issue, it may be helpful to explain the allowances available to officers.

Bayaran Imbuhan Wilayah (BIW) supports eligible officers serving outside their home regions. Bayaran Imbuhan Sara Hidup (BISH) is a cost-of-living allowance linked to locality, while Bayaran Insentif Mengikut Lokasi dan Tahap Kesusahan (BIMLTK) applies to designated facilities in remote or difficult areas, with rates determined by hardship level.
Under the current rules, BIMLTK is tiered, while BIW has fixed rates for newly eligible officers and protections for existing recipients.

One concern raised relates to BIW. Previously, the allowance was calculated as a percentage of salary. Following the change to a fixed-rate structure, some officers have seen their actual payments fall significantly.

BISH is determined by locality and officers’ grades, which may not accurately reflect actual living costs. Meanwhile, BIMLTK eligibility is tied to designated facilities rather than rural status alone.

The overarching concern is the lack of clarity over why an individual qualifies for, or is excluded from, a particular allowance. With different rules and arrangements being implemented, officers have little transparent information on how their entitlements are determined.

Therefore, the government should publish the relevant claim rules, required documents, processing deadlines and payment dates within the next fortnight, and allow advances to be paid before relocation.

Within the next three to six months, the government should establish a centralised digital service linked to ePlacement, allowing officers to check their entitlements, apply directly, upload documents once and track the progress of their cases.
It should also review the fixed BIW rate and assess remote sites across Sabah, Sarawak and qualifying parts of Perak, Kelantan, Terengganu, Pahang and Johor against consistent criteria.

In the longer term, the government should work with state governments to prioritise the repair and maintenance of health service residential quarters in rural and remote areas, while developing clear rural career pathways for doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers.

A coordinated, phased approach to these measures should help address the barriers preventing younger officers from taking up their postings. The issue should not be reduced to a question of willingness to serve, nor should it be attributed to a lack of interest or patriotism.
Over the past fortnight, the government has made several welcome commitments to the healthcare workforce, further reinforced by the 2027 Budget.
The next test is delivery: clear entitlements, timely relocation support, fair regional allowances and credible career pathways.
A posting letter can fill a vacancy only when the terms make the move possible — and give people a reason to stay.
